Question: What would have been a better plot for the Star Wars Sequel Trilogy?
Answer: What they’re starting to flesh out in the new canon books. While I’ve complained a lot about the world-building in the Star Wars sequels, I think in some ways their setting is quite interesting. A fascist Imperial rump state slowly building up arms while the New Republic is divided by bickering, forcing our heroes to take up underground armed resistance is a fascinating premise. It would also play off of the prequel trilogy in a fun way, as our heroes, rather than unconditionally serving a failed Republic, have realized that working outside of the system is the only way to affect change. Seeing this intergalactic confrontation play out would add some much-needed substance to The Force Awakens, help explain Luke’s absence, and would help differentiate the movie from A New Hope. A scene where the New Republic senate condemns Resistance leaders for engaging First Order troops on Takodana, while simultaneously failing to call out the First Order for invading the planet in the first place, would also help explain why Leia and Admiral Ackbar founded the resistance in the first place. These stories were glaring absent from the movies (the most accessible form of Star Wars content), and it’s very frustating that such a great storytelling opportunity was simply ignored. Hopefully though, these stories will be told in the new canon via books and comics as it begins to find its footing. Stay safe, -Ben

A story about a teacher in Rebel territory trying to design a school curriculum on a poor planet without adequate funding, with only outdated Imperial holotextbooks to use, would be so interesting. In conclusion- the non military aspects of the Rebel Alliance would be fascinating to see in more-depth. In the New Republic era, we see a well-developed, stable government. The US then hoped to offer the North Vietnamese food aid as a condition of surrendering. This is what Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton wrote of the plan[1]. Jane Fonda, Jean-Christophe Öberg (a Swedish diplomat), and even the UN Secretary-General verified that the United States had undertaken large-scale bombing of dikes.[2] This bombing focused on the Red River, where some 15 million peasants resided. In conclusion, the American bombing of Vietnamese dikes was a horrific war crime. Thankfully, their plan to starve the Vietnamese into submission failed. Question: Was Thomas Sankara a good president for Burkina Faso?
Answer: Yes. Thomas Sankara, known as the “African Che Guevara,” was a legendary leader of Burkina Faso. During his presidency, he drastically improved the lives of Burkinabe citizens and inspired countless people around the world to fight against oppression. But perhaps most impressively, he lived authentically and, unlike so many African leaders at the time, didn’t have a corrupt bone in his body. Thomas Sankara started his political career as an army captain. As he trained in various countries in Africa, Sankara witnessed brutal poverty and destitution. These experiences radicalized Sankara, and he became an idealistic socialist. Sankara quickly put his ideals into action, by forcing his army unit to socialize and integrate with the local population. His unit even formed an orchestra to play alongside civilians. These actions helped bridge the gap between the army and the Burkinabe people. When Sankara was made a minister in the (then dictatorial) Burkinabe government thanks to wartime heroics, Sankara continued this pattern of accountability and honesty. Sankara protected journalists from the repressive central government and biked to work, unlike most corrupt governmental officials who drove luxury Mercedes with dollars stolen from government coffers. Thanks to Sankara’s actions both as a minister and army officer, he soon commanded a large base of popular support. In 1983, the Burkinabe people rose against the central government and put Sankara as the president. Sankara began a wide range of reforms. These are some of them: -Increased literacy rates by 60%, from 13% to 73%, -Planted 10 million trees to successfully stop the southward spread of the Sahara Dessert -Ended River Blindness and Polio, and became the first African country to recognize and take action against AIDS. -Vaccinated millions of children in the first month of his presidency -Converted an army base into the nation's first supermarket -Sold the government fleet of Mercedes for Renault 5s, the cheapest car available in Burkina Faso at the time -Increased wheat production from 1,700kg/hectare to 3,800kg/hectare -Greatly reduced the amount of bush (rainforest) burning, which was very harmful to the environment -Appointed women to high government positions, encouraged and funded female education, ended polygamy, child marriage, and female genital multination Sankara even changed the name of Burkina Faso. Before Sankara’s presidency, the country had previously been named “Upper Volta,” a legacy of French colonialism. Sankara renamed the country “Burkina Faso,” which means “Land of the Upright Man.” This renaming was symbolic of the changes the country was going through. Many African countries, including Upper Volta, had been kept dependent on foreign aid by Western powers. Western companies and governments prevented many African countries from being self-sufficient. However, Sankara’s reforms ended Burkina Faso’s reliance on foreign aid and struck a blow to French colonialism by making Burkina Faso economically self-sufficient. And, given how Sankara eliminated the once-pervasive government corruption, renaming Upper Volta to “the land of the upright man” could not be a more fitting change. Indeed, Thomas Sankara was an upright man. Thomas Sankara rode his bike to work because he did not own a car. Sankara’s net worth was very little, and Sankara’s house was a small apartment near the capital building. Sankara even refused to own air-conditioning, because the majority of the Burkinabe people did not have air conditioning. This authenticity and solidarity won him the love and admiration people not just in Burkina Faso, but around the world. So, if Thomas Sankara was so amazing, why is Burkina Faso today not a shining example of socialist democracy? Well, because the snake of French colonialism was wounded but not dead. On October 15th, 1987, French and Malian foreign agents overthrew the government of Thomas Sankara and installed a tyrannical dictatorship. Unfortunately, almost all of Sankara’s reforms were rolled back. Poverty, gender inequality, and dessertification- all the issues Sankara fought against- rapidly became large issues in Burkina Faso again. However, there is still hope for the country. In September 2022, a coup occurred in Burkina Faso and a new government led by Ibrahim Traoré took power. Traoré has expressed admiration for Thomas Sankara and has opposed French colonialism. Traoré, in a very Sankara-esque move, even cut government salaries by 50% and is using that money to help refugees. It is unknown yet whether Traoré will go as far as Thomas Sankara did- but these policies show that even 36 years after his death, the memory of “Africa’s Che Guevara” lives on. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What is the difference between sex and gender?
Answer: Biological sex is a bimodal distribution of biological features. It is determined by a variety of factors, such as bone structure, chromosomes, genitals, and other physical features. Importantly, biological sex is determined by an amalgamation of these traits, not just one of them. Additionally, biological sex is bimodal, not binary. This fact means that if you were to plot people’s biological sex on a chart, the graph would have two peaks, but there would be people in between the two peaks. These people are frequently called intersex. This is a bimodal distribution, similar to biological sex. Gender is a set of societal and cultural norms that is expected of people of different biological sexes. It is an combination of various patterns, such as the clothes people wear, the way the do their hair, and the role that people play in society. Just as sex is not determined just be what genitals you have, gender is also not determined by any one trait. Gender norms have varied across cultures. Some cultures consider it very masculine to wear skirts, others consider it a feminine trait. In the United States, pink used to associated with boys, now the opposite is true. The point is, gender is a social construct, and while some aspects of gender may roughly align with traits associated with one biological sex or the other, gender is hardly a set-in-stone concept. People’s gender identities can also change over time. Troubles arise when we force people to align with the static gender identity that is assigned at birth. Since gender is a cultural and social construct, and sex is not binary, forcing people to express their gender identities in specific ways is harmful and dehumanizing. We need to accept everyone’s gender expression, even if it doesn’t match their biological sex. So, that is the difference between sex and gender. Remember, trans women are women, trans men are men, and nonbinary people are valid. These topics are much more nuanced and complicated than I could explain here, so I highly recommend you read up on these subjects from scientific sources (not Joe Rogan). Stay safe, -Ben

Question: How natural is capitalism to human nature?
Answer: Not natural at all. In our modern form, humans have existed on this earth for 100,000 years. During that time, we created different economic systems, from communal hunter-gatherer tribes to slavery to feudalism. Capitalism has only existed for 500 years. It is silly to believe that an economic system that has only existed for 1/2000th of humanity is somehow human nature. How did hunter-gatherers manage to feed themselves with no profit incentive??? This is, of course, assuming human nature is an inherent, static concept. Instead, human nature has a dialectic relationship with the world around us. Our material conditions, such as the economic system, the environment, and the availability of natural resources all affect and change human nature. Human nature, in turn, also affects the material conditions of society. No economic system can be “human nature,” because human nature changes and evolves. Besides, if capitalism is human nature, why does it require government bailouts every few years to stay afloat? From the Great Depression to the 2008 Financial collapse, capitalists have always depended on government assistance to protect their wealth. And if capitalism is human nature, how come the US government has had to intervene around the world to crush socialism and preserve capitalism? If not for US intervention, it is likely that anti-capitalist movements were have succeeded in Central America, Southeast Asia, and Southern Africa. An economic system that is supposedly human nature should not require military intervention every decade to keep existing. Examining capitalism’s roots can also show how it is far from human nature. Capitalism’s inception was marked by an incredible amount of violence and genocide. Capitalism was built on the murder of millions of indigenous Americans, the brutal colonization of most of Asia, and the slavery of millions of Africans. How can capitalism be human nature, when massive amounts of forceful coercion were required to birth it into existence? In conclusion, even if any economic system can claim to be human nature, capitalism remains far from human nature. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Is racism actually a quite natural aspect of human behavior?
Answer: No. Oftentimes, people trying to justify racism (and occasionally, misguided onlookers) will claim that racism is a natural aspect of human nature. These people believe that humans are naturally predisposed to fear and dislike people with different color skin and that this can explain structurally racist aspects of our society. This assertion, however, is built on a faulty premise and is completely ahistorical. First, race is not biological, but rather a social phenomenon. How many races exist, who is considered “white,” and so on have changed over time. Irish people, Jews, and Italians have at points not been considered white, and numerous scientists have proposed that as many as four to several dozen races exist. Racism, therefore, is primarily a result of social conditions, not biological reality. (I'll discuss what exactly these social conditions are later). If one examines history, one will find many examples of people of different “races” working together towards a common goal. Although for much of history blacks and whites have been pitted against each other, they have come together to work towards common goals remarkably frequently throughout history. From Bacon’s Rebellion to Fred Hampton’s Rainbow Coalition, history is littered with examples of black and white people working together despite the racial enmity present in their societies. (Such examples have also induced swift and severe reprisals from the status quo). Bacon’s Rebellion, pictured above, saw poor blacks and whites unite against wealthy landowners (and, unfortunately, Native Americans) Additionally, while humans may have some initial predisposition to be wary of people with different color skin, the presence of another human, in a similar situation to you, is far more powerful. The mere fact that laws had to be passed in Colonial America to prevent black and white people from fraternizing together[1] shows that racism, rather than being a natural aspect of human behavior, is often imposed from above. There is ample evidence to indicate that racism has been used by the ruling class to divide the working class. In Colonial America, the ruling planter class imposed laws putting poor whites slightly above enslaved blacks, as to prevent white and black people from rising against the wealthy. Lifting poor white people to a slightly higher societal position than blacks created a stable racial hierarchy that ensured the safety of the capitalist system[2]. Rather than facing the combined might of the white and black working class, the ruling class can sit back and watch poor blacks and whites fight each other over scraps. These work of pitting races against each other has at times been a result of an instinctual desire on the part of capitalists to protect profits, but has also been sometimes quite purposeful. For example, during a wave of strikes in 1919, steel corporations ordered their henchmen to do the following: We want you to stir up as much bad feeling as you possibly can between the Serbians and the Italians. Spread data among the Serbians that the Italians are going back to work. Call up every question you can in reference to racial hatred between these two nationalities; make them realize to the fullest extent that far better results would be accomplished if they will go back to work. Urge them to go back to work or the Italians will get their jobs.[3] In conclusion, racism is not natural. Instead, it is a result of an attempt by the ruling class to divide the working class, setting up a stable hierarchy to protect capitalism. It is incorrect to believe that an initial predisposition to be scared of those who look different could cause the mass genocide and enslavement that have resulted from racism. It is the system of economic classes that has characterized America since it’s inception that has caused racism, and in order to dismantle racism, we must move towards a classless society. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Did colonialism benefit or harm Africa?
Answer: Colonialism hurt Africa. The pernicious myth that colonialism helped Africa has become increasingly widespread lately. This fiction- the modern-day version of “white man's burden” purports that colonialism helped Africa because the European powers built infrastructure and brought modern technology to Africa. However, Africa was not a barbaric land devoid of technology before the European’s arrival, but rather an incredibly diverse continent full of advanced civilizations. In parts of Africa, societies had mastered C-sections and discovered inoculation against deadly diseases. Advanced states, such as the Regency of Algeria, the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, and the Empire of Mali existed, and different African civilizations created stunning cities, such as the Great Zimbabwe, Timbuktu, and Kilwa Kisiwani. In Ghana, real wages remained higher than in almost all of Northern Europe before colonialism. When the Europeans arrived and began the process of colonization, many of these advancements were destroyed. See, Africa has always been a rich continent- rich in both hardworking inhabitants and in natural resources. Africa’s labor force was stolen by European slavery (a process abetted by some greedy African tribal leaders) and many of Africa’s natural resources were stolen through colonialism. As a result, life expectancy, average height, and overall standards of living plummeted. When improvements in the quality of life for ordinary Africans occurred, they happened despite colonialism, not because of it. These improvements also largely happened during the 20th century, when anti-colonial movements were gathering steam. But the legacy of colonialism remains difficult to overcome (in part because colonialism never ended). In many parts of Africa, real wages and human stature have yet to recover from colonialism began[1]. In conclusion, colonialism drastically hurt Africa. It’s impossible to know what Africa would be like without Africa. But we can say for certain that colonialism hurt Africa, and it has only been thanks to the struggles of anti-colonial movements that some parts of Africa have recovered. Stay safe, -Ben *I also want to note that Africa is a massive and diverse continent, and colonialism impacted different parts in very different ways. However, overall, it has been scientifically proven that colonialism caused a downturn in living standards for ordinary Africans.

Question: Was Jimmy Carter a good President of the United States?
Answer: No. To understand Jimmy Carter’s presidency, its important to examine the 1960s and early 1970s. These years were a time of mass protests and disillusionment with authority. Student protests exploded during the 1960s, trust in the government plummeted, and the black-led, urban uprisings of the late 1960s posed the greatest threat to the established order since the strikes and labor unrest of the 1930s. Jimmy Carter worked to appease America’s populace, whose trust in government was shaken by America’s disastrous war in Vietnam and the Watergate scandal. Carter promised to cut the military budget, appointed women and people of color to some government positions, and funded some social services and green energy. But at the end of the day, Jimmy Carter still played within the acceptable norms of the American two-party system. Despite presenting himself as a humble farmer, Carter was a millionaire. To that end, Carter firmly protected corporate interests, such as in 1979 when Carter slashed corporate taxes while ordinary Americans suffered. Ultimately, the peanuts that Carter tossed ordinary Americans paled in comparison to his protection of wealthy elites. A similar theme was present in Carter’s foreign policy. Despite rhetoric about human rights, Carter consistently aligned the United States with tyrannical, far-right military dictatorships abroad. When Carter did advocate for human rights, these were never for egalitarian reasons. Carter advocated for South Africa to reduce its apartheid practices not because Carter hated racial inequality, but because a civil war in South Africa would threaten American mining interests. Similarly, while Carter did give aid to some famine-stricken African nations, Carter only did so to countries that pledged fealty to American hegemony and ignored the others. I’m sure people in East Timor, the Philippines, and Nicaragua would like to have a word with Carter about “human rights.” In conclusion, Jimmy Carter acted as a way for America’s ruling class to stabilize a system shaken by the revolutionary uprisings of the 1960s. Carter’s progressive policies were never undertaken out of a sense of altruism, but rather as concessions extorted out of the American establishment by the rebellions of the 1960s. And time and time again, Carter’s progressive policies were outweighed by his protection of corporate interests and American imperialism. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What is behind the Russian rhetoric about the "denazification" of Ukraine?

To that end, the Nazis encouraged their soldiers to kill, rape, and pillage with impunity. Wehrmacht soldiers were granted permission to murder any Russians suspected of anti-German sentiment. The Soviet economy was in shambles, and areas the size of entire countries had been completely razed by Nazi soldiers. But reports coming out of Ukraine of Neo-Nazi battalions and war crimes against ethnic Russians no doubt bring back deep-seated, institutional memories of the Nazi invasion of Russia. In conclusion, while Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is abhorrent, the country’s concern about Nazis in Ukraine is very real and reasonable. Question: Did the US really lose the Vietnam War or just left?
Answer: Yes, the United States lost the war. When the French withdrew from Vietnam in 1954, a communist government was created in the north and the United States supported an anti-communist government in the South, lead by Ngo Dinh Diem. Diem refused to elections to reunify Vietnam, because the vast majority of Vietnamese (around 80%) favored communism and reunification with the north. War broke out between North and South Vietnam in 1959, and the US slowly began committing more and more troops to Vietnam to prop up the crumbling South Vietnamese government. The Viet Cong rapidly began gaining support in rural villages, and it became clear that the United States, alongside its puppet government in Saigon, was fighting a war against the entirety of the Vietnamese people. Photo courtesy of the Guardian Slowly, both at home and abroad, the United States began to lose the war. At home, with casualties mounting and evidence of American atrocities reaching the public, a massive anti-war movement began, emerging from the civil rights movement and student activism. Abroad, the US barely managed to beat back the Tet Offensive and found itself fighting losing wars in Laos and Cambodia. Hoping to avoid to a complete embarrassment, the United States began Vietnamizing the war- withdrawing American forces while training and arming South Vietnamese troops. But because the South Vietnamese government was a US-backed puppet dictatorship, without a hand controlling the puppet, the puppet fell, and in April 1975 North Vietnamese troops liberated Saigon, ending the war. The argument that the United States did not lose but withdrew from the war crumbles when one realize that South Vietnam acted essentially as an American puppet, not an independent state. Though South Vietnam was supported by some nobility, it was widely detested, which is why the Vietcong gained so much support in rural, South Vietnamese villages. When the US withdrew from Vietnam, South Vietnam’s death warrant had been signed. “But what about casualty ratios?” People who claim that the US merely withdrew from Vietnam and did not lose to the war frequently point to the fact that for every 1 American killed, around 20 North Vietnamese were killed. However, as historian Howard Zinn writes, When the United States fought in Vietnam, it was organized modern technology versus organized human beings, and the human beings won. North Vietnam didn’t need to kill massive amounts of American troops. Vietnam was fighting on its home turf, and it simply needed to spill enough American blood to make the continued invasion not worthwhile. After 50,000 American troops and hundreds of thousands of South Vietnamese soldiers had been killed, the US finally withdrew. In conclusion, the United States lost the Vietnam War. It took decades, from fighting the Japanese to the French to the Americans, but by 1975, Vietnam was finally a unified, sovereign nation. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Are cops inherently bad?
Answer: In my opinion, yes. The slogan “All cops are bastards,” abbreviated “ACAB” or “1312,” has become popular in recent years. Many people have criticized this slogan, arguing that American police forces have some bad apples, but that many or most cops are genuinely good people. Some police officers are indeed good people outside of their jobs as police officers. However, every police officer has sworn an oath to enforce violent and cruel laws with violence if necessary, meaning that there are no good cops because the profession of “police officer” is inherently bad. The United States has many unjust and oppressive laws. In Florida, it is illegal to use a student’s preferred pronouns if the pronouns do not match the biological sex assigned at birth. 14 states prohibit abortion, and virtually every state has laws violent towards people who are homeless. Cops are also frequently called in to crush peaceful protests, break up strikes, and arrest political dissidents. Police officers cannot pick and choose which laws they enforce. By putting on their badge, police officers are promising to enforce every law, even ones that are cruel and tyrannical. Because of this fact, there are no good cops. During protests in Seattle in 1999, pictured above, police officers were ordered to use violent force against peaceful protestors, most of them teenagers. Many police officers sobbed before attacking the activists- but not a single cop stood down. This incident demonstrates how little individual morality matters compares to the systemic problems in policing. Because being a police officer entails participating in violent political repression, the job naturally attracts bad people. While not every police officer is a psychopath (I have met several police officers who are perfectly pleasant outside of work), cruel people and bullies are drawn to police work. 40% of police officers are domestic abusers[1], for example, a rate far higher than the general population. It is also true that police officers will sometimes do legitimately good work, beneficial for the community. But this occurs despite our modern system of policing, not because of it. There is no legal federal obligation for police to serve and protect, and helping out ordinary people comes second to violently enforcing the will of the state. The good work that police do can be better done by community-based organizations, rather than cops. Pictured above, police officers yesterday arrested several dozen skateboarders in San Francisco simply for participating in an annual skateboarding event. This mindless cruelty shows how for police, violent repression is a bigger priority than fighting crime. One example of how unnecessary police are could be found during the 1919 Seattle strike. A general strike paralyzed the city, including the police forces. Workers took over Seattle and began providing cheap meals to working-class families. Replacing the police force, workers organized patrols to keep the peace. Crucially, these patrols were forbidden from using force to keep the peace, they were only allowed to use persuasion. The commander of the U.S. Army unit sent into the area later stated that in forty years of military experience, he had never seen a city so orderly and quiet. When considering the 1919 Seattle general strike, it’s important to remember that the strikers’ system of police abolition only worked because capitalism had been (temporarily) dismantled, and people had their basic needs met. Workers had set up cheap, nonprofit food cafeterias, and 35 milk kitchens were also created. By meeting people’s basic human needs (a feat impossible under capitalism), the Seattle strikers were able to create a police-free society without chaos, violence, and disorder. In conclusion, the police are an inherently bad and unnecessary institution. While not every cop is a mean person, their job is based on violence and authoritarianism. It’s not difficult to imagine an egalitarian society in which people’s human needs are met and we don’t live under the repressive thumb of policing. Such societies have existed in bits and pieces in the past, and it is genuinely possible to create such a society today- if we get rid of the capitalist system that police protect. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What is the biggest myth about colonialism?
Answer: That it ended. When colonialism is taught in schools, it is often presented as a phenomenon of the past. Colonialism, we are told, ended in the second half of the second half of the 20 century and does not still exist today. After all, Kenya is not ruled by the United Kingdom, Vietnam is not controlled by France, and Mozambique freed itself from Portuguese domination. On paper, colonialism has ended. However, colonial empires of old have been replaced by neo-colonialism, an equally vicious yet less visible form of economic exploitation. Under neo-colonialism, independent countries in the global south are dominated politically and economically by multinational Western corporations. Even though these countries may be legally independent, with an army, national anthem, and flag of their own, they are kept subservient to Western colonial powers by the threat of economic sanctions and military interventions. Neocolonialism is most present in Africa. African countries are forced to sell their natural resources at low prices to Western companies. These companies then use these raw materials to create finished products, which they sell back to African markets at exorbitant prices. Because most African countries are prevented from creating industries of their own to compete with Western companies via this economic exploitation, African countries do not have an internal market for raw materials or finished products to compete with Western corporations. This gives Western multinational corporations what amounts to a monopoly over African markets. Western corporations parasitically suck 10 trillion dollars annually from Africa via this unequal exchange[1], ensuring ordinary Africans starve while Western executives live lives of luxury. And though this exploitation is (usually) not a result of any grand capitalist conspiracy, it is a result of capitalist’s primitive, subconscious profit-seeking interests. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) further exploits countries by giving out loans to struggling nations in exchange for “structural-adjustment programs.” In exchange for loans, countries are forced to liberalize and privatize their economy- essentially handing control of their national resources over to wealthy, foreign capitalists. In exchange, these countries are given shitty loans with high-interest rates, ensuring that these nations are trapped in debt ad infinitum. (China, to their credit, frequently gives out interest-free loans and recently forgave the debt of 23 African nations)[2]. Another way in which African countries are exploited is via unfair, colonial-era treaties For example, France forced their former colonies in west and central Africa to sign deals with France that tied their currencies to the Franc (and later the Euro), ensuring European dominance over much of Africa’s economies. France also forced their former colonies to grant Paris special access to natural resources and the right to station French troops in their countries, ensuring that France’s colonial empire remained intact in all but name. France enforces their neocolonialism with violence. Since 1960, France has invaded Africa 50 times and destabilized dozens of countries[3][4]. For example, when in 1960 anti-colonial leader Sekou Toure became president of Guinea and threatened France’s colonial empire, French agents flooded Guinea with counterfeit banknotes[5]. Decades later, a French agent bragged that Guinea's economy had yet to recover. France also backs dictators in Africa such as Idriss Deby. Despite an authoritarian and violent rule, Deby was trained and funded by France because he protected French economic interests in Africa until he died in 2021.[6] Unlike Deby, communist Thomas Sankara resisted the IMF’s exploitation and nationalized Burkina Faso’s natural resources, greatly raising the quality of life and achieving gender equality.[7] However, he was removed in a French-backed coup in 1987 and replaced by a nightmarish, authoritarian dictator, handpicked by the French government[8]. This barbaric policy of economic exploitation is undertaken by most Western countries. In 2011, Norway, the darling child of social democracy, brutally murdered civilians in Libya to protect its oil interests in the region[9][10][11][12]. The United States is probably the largest perpetrator of neocolonialism in the world, perversely undermining countries that resist this injustice (Nicaragua 1984[13], Honduras 2009[14], Bolivia 2019[15]). But unlike in Norway, where most everyone receives shares of the neocolonial loot via social welfare programs, in the United States, these plunders of war are reserved solely for the ruling class. Question: Has Capitalism allowed humans to have a high standard of living in recent decades?
Answer: For some people, yes First, we need to define capitalism. Capitalism is based on private property and the private ownership of production. Capitalism’s unique employer/employee relationship replaced the lord/serf and master/slave relationships of feudal and slave societies. Capitalism, in which a few business owners own the means of production, is contrasted with socialism, where the everyday workers own and operate the means of production. When capitalism arose in the 16th century, it did not immediately improve living conditions. Only in the late 19th century did significant improvements in the quality of life for people living under capitalist societies begin. As capitalism’s industrial societies emerged, access to indoor plumbing grew, life expectancy increased, and overall standard of living rose. However, these gains were not available to everyone. For one, capitalism’s imperialist invasions of other countries resulted in a significant quality of life decrease. In many indigenous communities, capitalism had a catastrophic affect on the standard of living. In some parts of the world, life expectancy has still not recovered from capitalist imperialism[1]. Additionally, to those most victimized by capitalism (the homeless, the incarcerated, etc) it’s pretty difficult to argue that capitalism has resulted in a better standard of living. The increased standard of living has been mostly for the upper and middle classes. Just enough people have just enough prosperity to prevent a revolution, while the ultra-rich get absurdly wealthy and the poor starve. The increases in living standards that did occur under capitalism were also largely a result of agitation by socialists and communists. When capitalism has historically impoverished millions, the rich have adopted reforms to prevent a socialist revolution. In the 1930s, when millions of Americans were thrust into poverty, the US government passed economic reforms that helped millions of people not out of the kindness of their hearts, but to prevent a communist revolution. And the gains of capitalism in Africa and Asia were accompanied by the massive growth of and agitation by anti-colonial movements. In addition, the increase in quality of life for some people is not a good justification for keeping capitalism as an economic system. Living standards for American slaves rose between the 18th and 19th centuries, however, despite this fact, it’s obvious to everyone why slavery needed to be abolished. A similar logic can be applied to capitalism. Although some people’s quality of life has increased under capitalism, capitalism’s barbaric relations of production render it indefensible. It’s simply unfair that workers under capitalism are stripped of their humanity and rendered human capitalism. It’s simply unfair that under capitalism, an employer has virtually totalitarian control over their employees. In order to remedy these unfair relations of productions, we need socialism. Socialism is based on economic democracy- workers democratically control their workplaces, instead of being controlled by the business owners. This economic system which prioritizes human needs over private profit, has increased the quality of life far beyond what capitalism has accomplished. A study[2] by Shirley Cereseto and Howard Waitzkin measured the quality of life in socialist and capitalist countries, an found that socialist countries consistently outperformed their capitalist counterparts. Socialist countries provided a higher daily per capita calorie supply as a percentage of requirement than did the capitalist countries at a similar level of development. The difference between capitalist and socialist countries averaged 12 to 15 per cent. Nutritional supply of all socialist countries exceeded the 100 per cent requirement In conclusion, although capitalism has improved the quality of life for many people, it remains an outdated system that must be abolished. As Martin Luther King said, “capitalism has outlived its usefulness.” Stay safe, -Ben

Question: How many US wars have been justifiable?
Answer: Very, very few. In this answer, I’ll be going through American wars and explaining why they were or were not justifiable. I should note that the US has been in a great many small wars and interventions, and for these, I’ll either be ignoring them or grouping them based on larger themes of the conflict, as it’s simply not possible to cover every American intervention in Latin America or Asia in sufficient detail. I’ll also won't cover the American Revolution, as I plan to discuss that in a separate, upcoming answer. Finally, I’ll be looking at whether the wars were morally justifiable, as the US has attempted to justify every war they have participated in, to varying degrees of success. American Indian Wars- Not justifiable The American Indian Wars, which began immediately after the American Revolution and ended in the early 20th century, were completely unjustifiable. They involved the United States invading Native American lands, violating treaties, and massacring civilians. Over time, this resulted in the genocide of most Native Americans and the relocation of the remaining ones onto small, poor reservations. War of 1812- Not justifiable The War of 1812 was primarily sparked by conflicts between British-backed Native Americans and US-backed settlers in the Ohio River valley along with the US’s desire to seize parts of Canada. Although the war was also caused by British impressment of American sailors, the mostly-expansionist origins of the war, along with US crimes against Native Americans, mean that the war was unjustifiable. Mexican-American War- Not justifiable The Mexican-American War began for several reasons. One cause of the conflict was the disputed border between Texas and Mexico- considering Texas had seceded from Mexico mainly to preserve slavery, Mexico was likely justified in this dispute, not the United States. Additionally, although the Mexicans fired the first shot of the war, the US had provoked the Mexican government into starting a conflict by occupying disputed territory just north of the Rio Grande. The Mexican-American War, therefore, was largely an unjustified expansionist conflict. The American Civil War - Justifiable The North was largely justified in fighting the Civil War. Although the South seceded because they wanted to keep slavery, many in the North initially fought the Civil War out of a desire to keep the Union together (many Northerners benefitted from slavery just as much as those in the South). However, as abolitionist pressure mounted and slaves in the South rose against their masters, the Civil War soon became a liberation war, in which hundreds of thousands of African Americans fought for their freedom against the slave-owning South. American interventions in Latin America pre-World War 2- Not justifiable Since the creation of the Monroe Doctrine in 1823, the United States has frequently intervened in the affairs of Latin America. The US intervened in Latin America often during the 19th century, but during the first half of the 20th century both the frequency and brutality of these interventions increased. According to historian Howard Zinn, between 1900 and 1933, the US intervened in Cuba four times, Panama six times, and Honduras seven times. All of these interventions were to protect American hegemony and protect markets for American exports overseas. Spanish-American War- Not justifiable The Spanish-American War was fought to protect US commercial interests in Cuba. The United States falsely blamed the mysterious explosion of the U.S. Maine, in port at Havana, on the Spanish government as a pretext to intervene in Cuba’s war against their Spanish occupiers. Rather than liberating the Cubans, however, the US imposed its hegemony on Cuba and occupied Puerto Rico and the Philippines, for no reason other than to protect American export markets- a common theme around the turn of the 20th century in American politics. Philippine–American War- Not justifiable Out of all the unjustified wars that the United States has fought, the Philippine-American is one of the worst-known wars and perhaps the most unjustifiable. The United States occupied the Philippines during the Spanish-American War but soon faced an insurgency led by Filipino nationalists. With overwhelming popular support, the rebels lead daring and deadly attacks on US troops. The US responded with depravity, massacring villages and slaughtering civilians en masse, all to protect their colonial possession. World War One- Not justifiable World War One was an imperialist conflict. France and the United Kingdom’s colonial empires were competing with that Germany and the dying Ottoman Empire, and hence war broke out. American companies invested heavily in the Allied side, and in 1917, with France facing mutiny and Russia being steamrolled, the United States decided to get involved to protect its corporate investments. This flimsy justification for conflict was accompanied by a German message to Mexico, encouraging Mexico to seize American territories in the west. However, the US had occupied the Mexican port of Veracruz several years earlier, and the United States had been clandestinely supporting the British and French for years. American Invasion of Russia- Not justifiable Only months after the Bolshevik revolution shook Russia and the world, American troops were already disembarking at Russian ports in the thousands. This effort was part of a larger Western intervention in the Russian Civil War, an attempt to “strangle Bolshevism in its cradle,” as Winston Churchill put it. This blatant war of aggression prolonged the Russian Civil War, lead to thousands of civilian deaths, and did not help the Russian people whatsoever. World War Two- Justifiable The United States participated in World War Two for all the wrong reasons, however, because they helped liberate Europe and East Asia from fascist occupation, their intervention was justified. The Allied powers, including the United States, did not go to war because of the heinous crimes of the Nazis or the Japanese Empire, but because the rising German and Japanese Empires threatened established imperial powers. This is why the United States did not go to war when Japan slaughtered thousands of civilians at Nanking, or when Germany announced their intentions to exterminate their Jewish minority, but only when the Axis empire threatened that of the United States. The United States’ actions during the war were also unacceptable. The United States imprisoned hundreds of thousands of Japanese citizens in internment camps and intentionally slaughtered innocent civilians by dropping the atomic bomb on heavily populated cities. However, because the fascist totalitarianism that the United States helped defeat was much worse than the admittedly-terrible Western imperialism that replaced it, the conflict was justified. Korean War- Not justifiable Many people believe that the Korean War began when North Korea invaded South Korea in 1950. However, the origins of the conflict are more complicated than that. After the Koreans threw off their Japanese occupiers in 1945, the United States divided Korea between the Soviet-backed North and the American-backed South. South Korea quickly became a fascist state, that brutally slaughtered communists and civilians alike in the hundreds of thousands. The US-backed South Korean government also sent terrorists to assassinate North Korean officials, nearly killing North Korean leader Kim Il-Sung. During the conflict, the United States also committed heinous war crimes. The US used biological weapons and killed millions of Koreans. At one point during the conflict, American pilots began firing their bombs into the ocean because they could not find a building in Korea undamaged by American munitions. Both the American entry into the war and conduct during the war were morally unjustifiable. Vietnam War- Not justifiable The Vietnam War was also unjustified. Ho Chi Minh leads the Vietnamese forces in successful liberation struggles against their Japanese and French occupiers. After the French were defeated, to slow the rising tide of communism, the United States divided Vietnam into two parts. Even though 80% of the Vietnamese supported communism, the United States did everything in its power to prevent the communists from winning the ensuing war between North and South Vietnam. Although the US poured thousands of troops and millions of dollars into defending the puppet dictatorship in South Vietnam, it was ultimately unsuccessful in defeating the will of the Vietnamese people. After decades of war crimes and Agent Orange, Vietnamese troops finally liberated Saigon in 1975, freeing the country from foreign occupation after 5 decades of struggle. American Cold War interventions- Not justifiable The United States engaged in many smaller military interventions during the Cold War, all of them unjustified. In the Dominican Republic, the US intervened to protect the military junta that overthrew democratically-elected president Juan Bosch. In Cuba and Grenada, the US invaded to overthrow a popular revolutionary government- failing in the case of the former, succeeding in the case of the latter. In Indonesia, Lebanon, Nicaragua, Panama, and other countries, the US intervened to protect its hegemony, leaving the countries it occupied worse off and the US more powerful. First Gulf War- Not justifiable In 1990, Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein launched an invasion of Kuwait to dodge debt payments owed to Kuwait and to capture valuable oil revenues. Hussein, who had been armed and encouraged by the US during the Iran-Iraq War, offered to withdraw from Kuwait in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal from Palestine, along with other minor demands. But the US was out for blood, and launched a powerful attack on Iraq, destroying Hussein’s military capabilities and reducing Iraq’s civilian infrastructure to a “pre-industrial level,” according to the UN. The conflict was entirely avoidable and in large part a result of American meddling in the Middle East. Yugoslav Wars- Not justifiable In 1992, a war broke out in the Balkans between Bosnian Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. After a peace deal agreed upon by all sides was sabotaged by the US, the situation deteriorated. Numerous crimes were committed by all sides, but especially by Republika Sprksa, which committed genocide against Bosniaks. The US intervened in Bosnia and did a surprisingly competent job of bringing the conflict to a close. However, the US also intervened during the Kosovo War in 1999. The US bombing campaign killed thousands of civilians and did not help bring the conflict to a close, unlike the intervention in Bosnia. Overall, the US’s role in prolonging the conflict in 1992 and the brutality of their attack on Yugoslavia in 1999 render the US intervention in Yugoslavia unjustifiable. War in Afghanistan- Not justifiable After the 9/11 attacks, the United States immediately invaded Afghanistan, which was mostly controlled by the Taliban at the time. Despite Taliban offers to turn over Osama Bin Laden, the US invaded the country anyway. Even anti-Taliban activists in 2001 were opposed to the US invasion, knowing that foreign intervention in Afghanistan would only further the Taliban’s popular support in the long run. They were correct. After two decades of war crimes and protecting the opium trade, the US withdrew from Afghanistan, leaving the Taliban in stronger control of the country than ever before. Iraq War- Not justifiable The Iraq War has been one of the best and most widely used examples of a war of aggression in recent years, and for good reason. The US lied, claiming that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction and ties to Al-Qaeda. The US successfully invaded Iraq and immediately privatized the nation’s oil. A civil war between Sunnis and Shiites soon erupted in occupied Iraq, and the country’s security situation deteriorated from there. The war in Iraq was solely motivated by America’s need for oil and hegemony, without regard for the millions of Iraqis caught in the crossfire. Wars against Libya and Syria - Not justifiable Two of America’s most recent, yet poorly-known wars are the ones in Libya and Syria. In 2011 and 2013 respectively, the US attacked Libya and Syria. In both cases, the US hoped rebels would overthrow dictators Muammar Gaddafi and Bashar al-Assad. However, the rebels that the US supported turned out to be worst than the dictators they were fighting. In Libya, where the rebels managed to defeat Gadaffi, the country descended into chaos, with open-air slave markets appearing in Tripoli. In Syria, Assad called on Russian and Iranian support to beat back the US-backed rebels, many of which had joined ISIS. Although the US did back the YPG, a Kurdish militia fighting for a more egalitarian society, this was out of practical necessity to fight ISIS, and after ISIS was defeated in 2017, the US jumped ship, leaving Kurds at the mercy of Turkey’s guns. Anyone else remember watching this missile strike on TV? The US’s interventions in Somalia and Yemen were similarly unproductive, at least from a humanitarian standpoint. In Somalia, US intervention hasn’t helped resolve the ongoing civil war and famine. In Yemen, the American military is more actively harmful, as US-backed Saudi troops continue to commit numerous crimes against civilians. In conclusion, the vast majority of US wars have been unjustifiable. Out of the 24 conflicts I mentioned, only 2 have been justified. A look back at history shows how for centuries, the United States has been a perpetrator of violence, hatred, and imperialism around the world. Happy fourth of July! Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Did Mussolini really make the trains run on time?
Answer: No. The idea that Mussolini made the trains run is a myth often spread sardonically by people saying that good things can come out of terrible situations (and occasionally, by fascist apologists). However, due to merciless strike breaking and repression of workers rights, trains in fascist Italy were often late. The myth that Mussolini made the trains run on time is largely a result of fascist propaganda. For example, in the early 1920s, a large scale rebuilding of Italy’s railways took place, coinciding with workers’ uprisings and factory seizures across Italy. Despite the fact that these accomplishments took place before Mussolini came to power in 1922, he still claimed credit for the rebuilding of Italy’s railways[1]. Also, while Mussolini did improve the railway services to select luxury villages in Northern Italy,[2] this project was primarily in order to impress foreign visitors, not to serve the average person. Because Mussolini, like Adolf Hitler in Germany, was supported by wealthy capitalists, Mussolini undertook a campaign of strike-breaking and privatization[3]. By destroying worker’s protections and rights, they had less of an incentive to make the trains run on time. Additionally, though railways were one of the few industries that Mussolini did not privatize, the general inefficiency created by privatizing industries likely made railways slower as well. In conclusion, Mussolini did not make the trains run on time. Benito Mussolini ran an empire based on slavery, racism, and exploitation, yet despite so much cruelty, he was unable to even make the trains run on time. Stay safe, -Ben

NATO’s bombing of Yugoslavia killed over 2,000 civilians in 1999 In addition, there are considerable numbers of Nazis within Ukraine’s military[4]. Question: What is your stance on prison abolition?
Answer: I support it. In order to understand why prisons must be abolished, we must understand the origins of prisons themselves. Prisons have not been the norm throughout humanity- in fact, prisons became commonplace only several hundred years ago. Prior to prisons, in feudal societies, punishment for a crime was mainly administered in violent and public ways- chopping off someone’s hand in front of a crowd, or a public hanging. However, when countries transitioned from a feudal society into a capitalist society emphasizing individual rights and private property, people began to view public corporal punishment as outdated and barbaric. Reformers argued that prisons, an environment in which the punished would be secluded from the public and were largely exempt from physical violence, was far more humane than corporal punishments. Hence, our modern prison system was born. Crucially, prisons originated due to changing societal conditions, namely the advent of private property and capitalism in the late 18th century. As a socialist, I believe that capitalism is an outdated economic system that should be replaced by socialism. Therefore, prisons should also be abolished as societal conditions change. I would like prisons to be replaced with restorative justice that focuses on repairing the harm done to the victim and rehabilitating the perpetrator. There’s no reason why someone who has committed a crime deserves to punished if that punishment does not help the perpetrator, the victim, or society. Restorative justice helps strengthen communities and focuses on helping the victim of crime, rather than punishing the perpetrator. Plus, our current capitalist system creates crime* and bad behavior in subtle ways. Capitalism’s system of private property stratifies society into two distinct classes: the owning class and the working class. Members of the latter, especially people of color, are impoverished by capitalism, forcing many to commit crimes for survival and destroying the social contract that keeps many people from committing crime. Mental illness is often left untreated in our capitalist system, and poverty oftentimes leads to drug addiction and homelessness, which can lead to even more crime, especially when homelessness is criminalized. Transitioning to a socialist system that prioritizes meeting people’s needs like housing and healthcare rather than private profits will reduce many of the behaviors that cause crime today. Many people who go into prison for non-violent offenses come out traumatized and later go on to commit violent crimes. Of course, no society in utopian, and in a socialist, prison-free society people will still commit horrific acts, like murder or sexual assault. However, capitalism fails to prevent these acts, and oftentimes actively encourages them. The glamorization of violence in our cultural milieu and the patriarchal system that characterizes modern gender relations induces violent crime and sexual assault. Transitioning to a socialist society free from gender hierarchies that culturally emphasizes community building over violence will reduce the amount of behaviors that are typically cited as necessary for prisons. Unfortunately, we can’t immediately abolish prisons, just as we won’t immediately achieve socialism. The prison-industrial system in the United States is titanic, as America proudly boasts the world’s largest prison population. However, emphasizing restorative justice and humane treatment of prisoners while attacking the capitalist underpinnings of our current criminal justice system are the first steps we can take towards moving to a prison free world. As humans, we’re better than prisons. We can find better solutions to our problems than throwing people into dungeons for decades. Taking a collective, community-based approach to solving our problems rather than a capitalist one is necessary for the human race to flourish, and that transformation should start in our criminal justice system. Stay safe, -Ben *Crime is a social construct that varies depending on the to however, in this case I’m using it to refer to acts that generally violate the social contract, such as stealing and murder.

Question: What are the flaws in capitalism?
Answer: Here’s one. Recessions. We’ve all lived through a recession. If not the 2008 Great Recession, than the recession caused by COVID-19 pandemic. And as we all know, recessions are incredibly awful events. Millions of people lose their jobs, supply chains break down, and life becomes measurably worse for people across the country. For example, the 2008 Great Recession caused 260,000[1] excess deaths from cancer alone because people lost access to health care. Even for the survivors of recessionary purges, life is still difficult. Recessions can be incredibly traumatic events, as there is a stigma associated with losing one’s job. The massive amounts of stress from recessions can exacerbate medical conditions, and many people suddenly find they can no longer afford home or car payments. However, capitalism treats these recessions as normal, and part of the market self-regulating itself. Go into any Econ 101 class, and they will talk about the recession is a natural part of the business cycle. According to capitalists, as wages and input prices rise, companies cut back on production and lay people off, creating a recession. Then, as input prices and wages fall, production expands again, and we leave the recession. Never mind the fact that life became significantly worse for millions of people, whose only crime was participating in the capitalist economy. If we want to move a society without these deadly recessions, we need socialism. Recessions happen because of the capitalist market. Employers cut workers wages to increase their own profits, preventing workers from purchasing goods and services capitalists. Employers are then begrudgingly forced to raise wages to allow workers to purchase things, before cutting those wages again. Only transitioning to a socialist economy where workers own the means of production will prevent these recessions. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: How does capitalism affect the media enterprise?
Answer: Capitalism has an incredibly interesting, and I’d argue corrosive, effect on media. Under capitalism, decisions are primarily motivated by profit. Companies make decisions on what will make them most money. For example, it is profitable for a factory under capitalism to dump industrial waste into a river, even if it means that communities downstream will suffer, because properly disposing of industrial waste is more expensive than just tossing it into a river. As a result of this profit motive, capitalist media becomes bland, milquetoast reboots with very little uniqueness to it. Under our capitalist economy, Disney now produces boring, live-action remakes of old films rather than new and creative movies, because producing endless Lion King and Pinnochio remakes (and now a live-action Moana film) will make more money than trying a risky new product. No piece of media ever seems to die, which means no media can ever really live. Similarly, capitalist media supports the selling of commodities. For example, Paw Patrol, one of the most watched kids TV shows of all time, exists, let’s face it, to sell toys (and to force-feed a highly propagandized version of the police) to young kids. For some god-forsaken reason there’s even a Barbie TV show. Under capitalism, many pieces of media become about selling a commodity to people, especially to vulnerable audiences like little kids. It’s through institutions like these that capitalism enforces it’s power- not through violence, but through a cultural hegemony. But just as bland, profit-seeking media pieces become ubiquitous under capitalism, anti-capitalist messages can also make their way into TV shows. As late-stage capitalism deteriorates and more people become class-conscious, anti-capitalist ideas become more common in the media. Severance, for example, is a modern example of an anti-capitalist TV show. Parasite, which won Best Film at the Oscars a couple years ago, details the parasitical relationship between the working class and the capitalist class. And, to use an older example, Star Wars was originally a critique of American imperialism in Vietnam. The reason for this contradiction between capitalist and anti-capitalist media can be found if one takes a look at the work of Karl Marx. Karl Marx described how the economic base of society- it’s means and relations of production- affect the societal superstructure, which comprises things like politics, religion, government, and media. That societal superstructure in turn affects the economic base of production. In a society with a capitalist mode of production dominated by the bourgeoisie, there will logically be a societal superstructure that supports bourgeois interests and reinforces the capitalist mode of production. However, because the vast majority of people in the world are the working class, that working-class struggle will find its way into modern-day media, which may help radicalize people against capitalism. Thus, the contradiction between capitalist and anti-capitalist media occurs. So, that is how capitalism affects the media. I also want to add that in a capitalist society where people work 40 hours or a more a week, many people have little time and energy to produce truly meaningful art and media. Many people are so exhausted they only have the ability to passively consume. That’s why, under a socialist society where technological innovations are used to reduce working hours rather then generate profit, there will be an explosion of art and media and culture. People will simply have more time and energy to create truly beautiful artwork, not sit back and watch consumerist propaganda when they get off from work. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Is Alex Mann right about socialism and capitalism?
Answer: No. So, Alex Mann recently wrote an answer to the question “What is better: capitalism or socialism?” Mann’s answer received 100,000 views and almost 2,000 upvotes. And while his argument is made in good faith, it’s also demonstrably false, as I’ll show today. I’d also recommend you first read Mann’s answer here to make sure I’m not misrepresenting his arguments. Additionaly, all my sources will be linked below. Before responding to the answer, I’ll need to define socialism and capitalism. Socialism is worker ownership of the means of production, either through democratically-organized workplaces or through a democratic, worker-lead centrally-planned economy. Capitalism is private ownership of the means of production. Whereas everyone controls their workplace under socialism, under capitalism, only a few people control the means of production for everyone. Hence, capitalism has an authoritarian workplace structure and socialism has a democratic workplace structure. Under capitalism, goods are distributed based on who can afford them. If you can’t buy bread, you’re out of luck. Under socialism, goods are distributed based on need. A hungry family will still be given food to eat, even if they have no money to afford it. Firstly, Alex Mann brings up the example of Sweden. Mann states that Sweden was socialist in the 1970s-1990s, when it suffered slow economic growth. Then, it became capitalist, and became wealthier. However, Sweden was never socialist. Socialism is not when the government does stuff, it’s a complete reorganization of society around meeting the needs of the working people. Private enterprise and a capitalist redistribution of goods has always existed in Sweden. Social-democratic reforms are not socialist, they are capitalist. Now, how did Sweden become so wealthy? Simple. They started exploiting the global south[1]. Swedish multinational corporations own sweatshops across the world, extracting value to ensure Sweden stays rich and other countries stay poor. Sweden could not have such a high quality of life without children starving in sweatshops in Bangui, Dhaka, and Kinshasa[2], because capitalism is fundamentally exploitative. Mann asserts that socialism requires authoritarianism. Firstly, what is authoritarianism? A small group of people owning all the means of production around the world sure sounds like authoritarianism to me, especially contrasted to a democratic system of worker-self management. Capitalist dictators like Adolf Hitler, Augosto Pinochet, and Suharto sure seem authoritarian to me as well. Speaking of authoritarianism, part of my family is from Algeria. Algeria was colonized by the French, who brutally exploited the country, murdering millions and keeping the rest impoverished. This colonialism was a direct result of capitalism’s need for greater profits, and it was certainly authoritarian. Now, Mann brings up Cuba. Cuba is an important topic that takes a lot of time to cover, but I’ll briefly run through Mann’s points about Cuba. But before that, consider that Cuba has been under economic blockade by the most powerful country in the world for sixty years. The fact that Cuba is not literally the poorest country in the world right now is a testament to socialism, in that it has been able to resist terrorist attacks, invasion, and economic strangulation from the United States for longer than probably all of you have been alive. The goal of these sanctions, according to official US documents, was to “call forth a line of action which, while as adroit and inconspicuous as possible, makes the greatest inroads in denying money and supplies to Cuba, to decrease monetary and real wages, to bring about hunger, desperation and overthrow of government.”[3] Now, for some achievements of Cuba. -Cuba has a longer life expectancy than the United States[4][5] -Cuba has a lower infant mortality rate than the United States[6] -Cuba has a higher literacy rate than the United States[7] -Cuba exports doctors and teachers for free[8][9]. For example, Cuban doctors in Brazil provide life-saving healthcare to 28,000,000 people[10] -Cuba hosts thousands of impoverished foreign students[11] -Cuba has the most doctors/capita in the world[12] -Cuba has the most sports instructors/capita in the world[13] -Cuba has the most art teachers/capita in the world[14] -Cuba helped liberate Africa from colonial oppression[15] -According to the United Nations Sustainable Development Index, Cuba has a higher quality of life than the United States, the wealthiest country in the world[16] Now, Mann tries to state that some countries are “x amount socialist, y amount capitalist.” Ignoring the fact that Mann is pulling these numbers out of his ass, Mann fails to understand that a country cannot be simultaneously capitalist and socialist. They are mutually-exclusive economic systems. Just as you cannot be 35 years old and 60 years old, you cannot be both capitalist and socialist. More information here. Mann also talks about North Korea. North Korea was bombed to the dirt during the Korean War[17], and then hit with massive economic sanctions. Meanwhile, South Korea was given lucrative trade deals and was opened up to western development. The comparison is hardly fair. Mann asserts that socialism has been tried and failed. I debunk this claim in more detail here, but I’ll leave three academic studies for Mann to ponder. The first two shows that socialist countries have had better healthcare than capitalist countries. The second shows that socialist countries have routinely had a better quality of life than comparable capitalist countries, time and time again. "Socialist countries provided a higher daily per capita calorie supply as a percentage of requirement than did the capitalist countries at a similar level of development. The difference between capitalist and socialist countries averaged 12 to 15 per cent. Nutritional supply of all socialist countries exceeded the 100 per cent requirement."[18] It is a demonstrable scientific fact that socialist countries have provided their citizens a better quality of life than capitalist countries[19]. Alex Mann also states that capitalism is working. He points out that deaths from preventable disease, poverty, and war are going down. To some extent this is true, but that has largely been despite capitalism, not because of it. Additionally, given that 40 million Americans are in poverty[20], food insecurity is drastically increasing around the world[21], fascism is on the rise[22], we are on the brink of nuclear war[23] and climate change is threatening organized human existence[24], it’s pretty hard to argue capitalism is working. Mann asserts that “We are never going to have a utopia where everyone eats and is happy. “ as if ending world hunger is some impossible goal. However, we produce enough food to feed 10 billion people[25]. However, under capitalism, those who cannot afford food do not eat, so as a result we have world hunger. Under socialism, everyone would be guaranteed the human right to 3 decent meals a day, regardless of their ability to afford it. Finally, Mann makes a series of 7 short points supporting capitalism. I’ll run through them and debunk them as fast as I can. In conclusion, Alex Mann is wrong about socialism and capitalism. Socialism is the superior economic systems, and the arguments against it, as Mann demonstrates, range from Cold War-era propaganda to outright classism. I’m also sorry this answer was so much longer than I expected- it takes 10 minutes to debunk a 10 second lie. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Is there any correlation between fascism and capitalism?
Answer: Yes. I’m getting really tired of people saying that fascism is somehow socialist, or that fascism is not capitalism. However, it is an objective, empirical, observable fact that fascist countries have had a capitalist economic structure. It is also an objective, empirical, historical fact that wealthy capitalists have backed fascist movements across the world specifically because they were afraid of rising socialist movements. It is also a objective, empirical fact fascists have ruthlessly hunted socialists and communists to virtual extinction in their respective countries. Firstly, I want to make sure we’re on the same page about what fascism and capitalism are. Fascism is palingenetic ultranationalism that prioritizes hierarchy, authoritarianism, strength, the military, and genocide. Examples of fascist countries are Italy under Mussolini, Germany under Hitler, and Chile under Pinochet. Capitalism is the private ownership of the means of production- that is, employers control the workplaces and their employees. This is in contrast to socialism, where workers- the employees- own their businesses. (No, socialism isn’t when the government does stuff). Now, fascist countries privatize businesses. Privatization is when government-owned industries are sold off to private industries. It is the one of the most capitalist economic policies possible. And fascists privatize all the time. Though it wasn’t called privatization at the time, Mussolini privatized life insurance, telephone services, and machinery factories[1]. The word “privatization” was virtually invented to describe Hitler’s economic policies[2][3]. Chile, which was ruled by fascist dictator Augusto Pinochet for decades, became the archetype for neoliberal privatization[4]. Secondly, wealthy capitalists support fascists all the time. The Federazione Industriale, a collection of powerful Italian industrialists, donated 20 million Lira[5] to fund Mussolini’s March on Rome. I.G. Farben and Krupp[6] provided a wealth of funds to the Nazis, and Pinochet’s regime was backed by the Chicago Boys[7], a group of American-trained economists who supported neoliberal privatization. All of these examples came during time of rising socialism. In Italy, socialist and anarchist groups were becoming more popular as workers, disillusioned by the horrors of World War One, turned to leftist politics. In Germany, the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) was on the rise, and the memories of the 1919 communist rebellion in Germany were very fresh in people’s minds. In Chile, Salvador Allende, a Marxist, had just been elected president. Capitalists were terrified of the rising socialism, and so backed fascists. The fascists returned the favor by privatizing countless industries. Salvador Allende, kalashnikov in hand, attempts to stave off the forces of Augusto Pinochet And, of course, these fascists persecuted anti-capitalists relentlessly. Mussolini’s brownshirts assassinated labor organizers and trade unionists, and locked up anarchists and socialists. The first victims of Hitler’s concentration camps were communists and anarchists. And Pinochet’s regime became notorious for dropping leftist dissidents out of helicopters. In conclusion, fascism is a capitalist ideology. It supports private business and ruthless murders anti-capitalists. Stay safe, -Ben *While it is true that fascist governments have occasionally nationalized industries, these came during times of war when other countries, also at war, nationalized industries. Just as Harry Truman nationalized steel mills during the Korean War did not make him a socialist, neither did Hitler or Mussolini nationalizing an industry or two during World War 2.

Question: What's the worst war crime that no one knows about?
Answer: The sanctioning of Iraq from 1991–2003. In 1991, the United States (US) fought Iraq after Iraq had invaded Kuwait* in what became known as the First Gulf War. The US routed Iraqi troops and liberated oil-rich Kuwait. During the conflict, the US dropped massive amounts of bombs on Iraq, relegating Iraq to a “pre-industrial age[1],”, according to the United Nations (UN). The US then withdrew from Iraq, allowing Saddam Hussein, the Iraqi dictator, to remain in power. However, although the US did withdraw it’s troops from Iraq, it did not leave the country alone. The US and the United Kingdom imposed numerous no-fly zones and sanctions on Iraq. The sanctions in particular were devastating towards Iraq’s economy. Without their ability to rebuild civilian infrastructure, millions of Iraqis went without food or water, and the Iraqi healthcare system was devastated[2]. The Iraqi sanctions were aimed to make the Iraqi population hungry, which the US hoped would force them rebel against Saddam Hussein. However, the opposite happened. Although millions of Iraqis starved, the sanctions forced them to depend more on Saddam Hussein, and furthered the reach of his dictatorship. The human cost of the Iraq sanctions are difficult to quantify, but they are massive. By 1995, the UN[3] was reporting that 500,000 Iraqi children had been killed by the sanctions. Many more likely died in the next 8 years, not to mention the millions that were forced to go without food or shelter. Of course, this humanitarian catastrophe hardly seemed to affect American leadership. In 1996, when asked about whether the deaths of 500,000 Iraqi children were worth it[4], then-Secretary of State Madeline Albright replied with a resounding “yes.” The sanctions would only be brought to an end by the Iraq War, when the US, after falsely claiming Iraq possessed WMDs, invaded Iraq. This invasion sparked a decades-long civil war and the flaring up of Sunni-Shia relations, the consequences of which are still being felt today.
