Question: What is Noam Chomsky's propaganda model?
Answer: Noam Chomsky’s propaganda model, discussed in his book Manufacturing Consent, is a theory for how the US mass media will cover different events. By analyzing how various aspects of the US mass media such profit incentives and right wing NGOs affect the US mass media, Chomsky creates a propaganda model that reasonably analyzes how mainstream news outlets will cover different events. It should be noted that Chomsky does not believe that there is not any serious, intentional malicious manipulation of the US mass media. Rather, the affects of capitalism create a culture of self-censorship and unintentional filtering that limits the diversity of views present in the US mass media. It’s also important to note that when the US mass media lies, it is usually by omission. Additionally, I should note that a trained, intelligent reader can find and put together details from the US mass media that are harmful to the US government and capitalism as a whole- it’s just difficult. With that out of the way, let’s look at the five ways that, according to Chomsky, the US mass media is filtered. Initial Funding This filter is by far the easiest to understand. Basically, it costs a lot of money to start a newspaper. While citizen journalism and social media are slowly changing this fact, it still costs a massive amount of money to start a professional, well-read news outlet. Therefore, only groups with large amounts of money on hand can start news networks, which limits the diversity and scope of news outlets present. Advertisements Advertisements greatly help a newspaper, because with advertisements, a newspaper can afford to print more newspapers and hire more journalists. Advertisements give newspapers a large competitive advantage. However, advertisements will only give money to a newspaper if they believe that newspaper’s readers can afford to purchase their products. Therefore, newspapers that cater to wealthy audiences (ahem, the Wall Street Journal) will get a competitive advantage. Government reliance Many larger newspapers heavily rely on the government for sources. In the incredibly competitive and high speed world of political journalism, having access to press conferences or certain sources can make or break a journalist’s career. However, news outlets that publish information too critical of the government will often lose access to government sources or exclusive news conferences. This reliance on official sources neuters the ability of mainstream American media to be critical of the US government. Flak In the world of air-to-air combat, flak is pieces of foil used to disrupt and confuse the radars of enemy fighter jets. In the world of journalism, flak plays a similar role. Flak, in journalism terms, is lawsuits, boycotts, and government repression used to stifle journalistic expression. Far-right NGOs (non-governmental organizations) will threaten any news outlet they perceive as leftist or centrist with boycotts and lawsuits. To smaller left-wing news outlets, this flak can be incredibly disruptive. Freedom House is one such NGO Similarly, the US government will often try to repress news organizations that publish information critical to the state. For example, the Nixon Administration tried to drown the Washington Post in lawsuits and threats in order to stifle the Watergate story. More disturbingly, the US government has arrested and imprisoned Julian Assange for reporting on US war crimes in Iraq. These examples of government repression will also prevent many more journalists from speaking up out of fear. Anti-communism Noam Chomsky and Edward Hernan describe anti-communism as a “national religion.” Chomsky and Hernan are correct. Any news outlet that doesn’t completely demonize communism is portrayed as the ultimate personification of evil. Historically, this has been due in large part to government repression (See: McCarthyism) but anti-communism has also become a large part the capitalist cultural hegemony. Anti-communist myths (communism goes against human nature, Stalin killed more people than Hitler, etc) have become widely believed, which seeps its way into the media. Propaganda Model These filters combine to form the propaganda model. Governments and groups allied with the United States government are portrayed positively. Governments opposed to the United States are demonized. Neoliberal capitalism is upheld, socialism is demonized. One example of how the mass media does this is through its portrayal of worthy and unworthy victims. Victims of atrocities by American client states are either ignored or were implied to have deserved their fate, while victims of atrocities by groups that go against American interests are spotlighted time and time again. This table[1] shows the media’s use of the word “genocide” whilst covering various genocides in the 1990s. The word genocide is rarely aimed at countries allied with American interests- the Indonesia, Turkey, the US itself- while it is levied heavily against countries that contradict American interests, like Serbia and Iraq*. More specific examples can be found in Manufacturing Consent, by Noam Chomsky and Edward Hernan. The book is fantastic and is a super engaging read- I cannot recommend it highly enough. Stay safe, -Ben *The attacks carried about against Bosniaks and Kurds by the Republika Srpska and the Iraqi government respectively were both horrendous genocides, and the importance of knowing about these atrocities cannot be overstated. However, the US mass media considered the Bosniaks and Iraqi Kurds to be “worthy” victims, while the East Timorese, Turkish Kurds, and Iraqi civilians were considered unworthy victims in a manner that furthers the interest of U.S. foreign policy.

Question: What is the incentive to work hard under socialism?
Answer: Improving one’s own life. Firstly, let’s define socialism. Socialism is the worker ownership of the means of production. That means all the factories and shipyards and industries are all owned by the employees, rather than by a few employers. Workplaces are organized by democratic principles, allowing workers to vote on what they produce, when they do it, and for how much they do it for. Also under socialism, goods are distributed based on need, rather than profit. Under capitalism, only those who can afford food, housing, and higher education can acquire them. Under socialism, the human rights to food, housing, and education are all guaranteed. These changes, however, do not eliminate the incentive to work. Firstly, under capitalism, work is seen as a painful chore that you have to do. The drudgery of labor present under capitalism is not a characteristic of work in general, merely of capitalism. Humans generally like being productive, we just don’t like being exploited under capitalism. When you aren’t forced by threat of starvation to stand at a low-paying job for eight hours a day, and when workplaces are controlled by the laborers, work will become a lot more fun. For example, if capitalism was eliminated, and the threat of becoming homeless or starving was removed, I wouldn’t sit around all day doing nothing. I would do something I enjoy, like gardening, or designing cities, or writing. I like work, just not being exploited. Additionally, while under socialism we would all be guaranteed a decent standard of living by virtue of being human, we would not be automatically entitled to every luxury in the world. While a three healthy meals a day would be a human right, no one would not be entitled to gourmet meals all the time. People would need to work to obtain luxuries, and to constantly seek a higher standard of living. That said, people would still work less under socialism. And that’s a good thing. See, a lot of jobs under our capitalist system is pointless. Corporate lobbyists, credit card vendors, police officers, and hundreds of other jobs are useless for everyone but the very wealthy. This problem is incredibly widespread. For example, 37% of Britains[1] don’t even think their jobs are at all useful. If we were to have those people work actually meaningful jobs, it would mean less work for all of us, without decreasing productivity. The same applies to automation. Under capitalism, a machine taking someone’s job is cause for concern- how will the now-unemployed worker sustain himself without a reliable source of income? Under socialism, a machine taking someone’s job would be cause to celebrate- less work for all of us! After all, since the 1930s, we have had more technological innovations than we could ever dream of. But under capitalism, working hours haven’t been cut once. Lastly, a transition to socialism will cause art and culture to flourish. Under capitalism, majoring in music or writing or theater is discouraged, because it is difficult to find well-paying jobs that utilize those skills. Under a socialist economy, where everyone is guaranteed food, housing, and education, future salaries won’t be a barrier to would-be artists and musicians. The explosion of music and theater and art that will follow a transition to socialism will be a sight to behold. In conclusion, under socialism, there will be motivation to work hard. We just won’t be working pointless, soul-sucking jobs with the anvil of homelessness and starvation hanging over our heads. But if we want to see a better future for the next generation, where kids don’t starve on the street while billionaires buy their fifth home, we’ll need to fight for it. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Was the atomic bomb necessary in Japan?
Answer: Absolutely not. The dropping of the atomic bomb was completely unnecessary and did not meaningfully affect the outcome of the war. Many supporters of the decision to drop the atomic bomb on Japan assert that had the United States not dropped the atomic bomb on Japan, a ground invasion would have been necessary to defeat Japan, which would have cost millions of lives. While a ground invasion of Japan would have been far deadlier than the atomic bomb, the atomic bomb did not force Japan to surrender. See, the United States had already destroyed dozens of Japanese cities through vicious firebombing that killed hundreds of thousands of civilians and displaced millions more. Countless Japanese cities had found themselves vaporized by American bombs within hours prior to the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The atomic bomb did not meaningfully change the balance of the war. Now, why did the Japanese empire surrender? Well, the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria on August 9th, 1945. The Soviet Union had a nonaggression pact with the Japanese Empire that was not due to expire until 1946. Japan was hoping that the Soviet Union would negotiate a tolerable peace between them and the United States, in part because the Soviet Union had refused to sign the Potsdam Declaration. Once Japan realized the Soviet Union was against them, they realized any hope for a negotiated peace was impossible. Of course, the United States had removed the Soviet Union from the Potsdam Declaration, because the United States worried that the Soviet Union would seek greater concessions in the far east after the end of the Second World War. There are many arguments that the atomic bomb was necessary- too many to respond to here. However, no matter how you defend the dropping of the atomic bomb, you cannot defend dropping it in the middle of a densely populated city. If the United States just had to drop the atomic bomb, they could have dropped it on a more isolated military target, or invited Japanese delegates to watch a controlled test of the bomb. Dropping it in the middle of a city is inexcusable. Most senior American generals at the time were opposed to the dropping of the bomb. It is my opinion that the use of this barbarous weapon at Hiroshima and Nagasaki was of no material assistance in our war against Japan. The Japanese were already defeated and ready to surrender because of the effective sea blockade and the successful bombing with conventional weapons. -Fleet Admiral Chester W. Nimitz It always appeared to us that, atomic bomb or no atomic bomb, the Japanese were already on the verge of collapse. - Air Force General Hap Arnold I voiced to him my grave misgivings, first on the basis of my belief that Japan was already defeated and that dropping the bomb was completely unnecessary, and secondly because I thought that our country should avoid shocking world opinion by the use of a weapon whose employment was, I thought, no longer mandatory as a measure to save American lives. It was my belief that Japan was, at that very moment, seeking some way to surrender with a minimum loss of “face.” -General Dwight D. Eisenhower Employment of the atomic bomb in war will take us back in cruelty toward noncombatants to the days of Genghis Khan. . . . in being the first to use it, we had adopted an ethical standard common to the barbarians of the Dark Ages. -Admiral William D. Leahy -Stay safe, -Ben *This answer is not meant to be a defense of the Japanese Empire. During the Second World War, Japan was a fascist dictatorship that committed numerous abhorrent war crimes. However, the actual civilian population of Japan was not necessarily complicit in the crimes their government committed, and did not deserve to have a nuclear weapon dropped on them. Question: Were the Soviets and Nazi Germany really allies before Operation Barbarossa?
Answer: No. The Soviet Union was not Nazi-allied. The Nazis and Soviets were bitter enemies, and the Soviet Union firmly opposed the Nazis whenever possible. To start, the Soviet Union funded anti-Nazi resistance fighters in Germany. Antifaschistische Aktion, the militant wing of the Communist Party of Germany, fought street battles against the Nazis. These heroes were funded and supplied by the Soviet Union. The same applies to the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia, a Comintern organization that waged a guerilla campaign against their Nazi occupiers beginning in 1938. The Soviet Union also opposed the Nazis during the Spanish Civil War. The Soviet Union sent guns, ships, and volunteers to support the Republican cause, while the Nazis set soldiers to fight for the Nationalists. The Soviet Union also volunteered to fight Nazi Germany on multiple occasions prior to the outbreak of World War Two. For example, the Soviet Union volunteered to go to war with Nazi Germany to protect Czechoslovakia in 1938[1], but Czechoslovakia refused the offer, as France was unwilling to go to war. The Soviet Union also volunteered to go war with Nazi Germany in August 1939. The Soviets reached out to Poland, Britain, and France and asked to form an anti-Nazi alliance[2]. The USSR even pledged to donate 1,000,000 troops to fight the Nazis. However, the Western Allies snubbed the Soviet Union by ignoring their request. Hitler also hated the Soviet Union. Believing that the USSR was run by inferior communist Jews, Hitler was ideologically opposed to the Soviet Union. The Nazis even created an agency called “Anti-Komintern” to disseminate anti-Soviet propaganda. Nazi propaganda frequently attempted to paint communism as a Jewish plot to destroy Germany So why did the Soviet Union sign the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact? Well, the Soviet Union believed that the Western Powers were not willing to go to war with Nazi Germany, and the Soviet Union was scared of a Nazi invasion. The Soviet Union was still industrializing, and needed more time to prepare for a solo war against Nazi Germany. Additionally, the Soviet Union wanted to protect Poland’s Jews from the Nazis. The Soviet Union was a pioneer in fighting anti-semitism (Lenin famously decried anti-semitism[3] as a capitalist plot to turn workers against each other). The Soviet Union understood that the Nazis would invade Poland whether or not the Soviets did as well. By occupying half of Poland, the Soviets were protecting the Jews in Eastern Poland country from the Nazis. And although it’s true that the Nazis and Soviets signed trade agreements and trained each other’s pilots, such behavior was commonplace among European countries and did not reflect any friendship between the two countries. In conclusion, the Soviets and Nazis were ideology opposed. The Soviets opposed the Nazis whenever possible, and the two were bitter enemies. Solidarity forever, -Ben

Question: Is it fair to say that socialism as a system has always failed when it was implemented?
Answer: No. Anti-communists, from far-right reactionaries to social democrats, have put forward the assertion that communism or socialism has “failed” every time it has been tried. However, this argument is unconvincing and nonsensical for several reasons. To start, let’s define socialism and capitalism. Capitalism is the private ownership of the means of production, usually characterized by markets and corporations. Class divisions between the owning class and the working class are stark. Socialism is the common ownership of the means of production without class divisions. Firstly, while capitalism has had many centuries to develop and expand, socialism has only existed for 150 years- the first “dictatorship of the proletariat” was the 1871 Paris Commune. Socialists have objectively had less time to develop their economic theories and practices than capitalists have. For this reason, we should be more generous when considering failures of socialist countries than capitalist countries. Additionally, socialists constantly try to improve their socialist experiments. Leftists practice self-criticism to a fault, and are constantly improve=ing their societies. For example, Thomas Sankara’s agricultural collectivization (more on that later) in 1983 Burkina Faso proceeded far more smoothly than Stalin’s policies, because Sankara learned from the successes and failures of collectivization in Soviet Russia. Judging modern day socialism on the failures of century-old socialist experiments fails to recognize how socialist thought develops over time. Additionally, the claim that socialism or communism has failed every time does not take into account what determines success and failure. Does a country need a powerful military to be successful? Strong political freedoms? Excellent healthcare? Food security? I argue that a successful country is one that has a solid quality of life, impressive political freedoms, and a lack of discrimination based on gender, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, etc. Socialist countries have overwhelmingly demonstrated a superior ability to meet these criteria than capitalist countries. Quality of Life Socialist countries, on average, have created a better quality of life for their citizens than capitalist countries. There is empirical evidence to back up this assertion. The study Economic Development, Political-Economic System, and the Physical Quality of Life[1], which measured indicators like life expectancy, caloric intake, and literacy rate, showed that socialist countries had better quality of life indicators than capitalist countries of equivalent economic development levels 28/30 times. In 16/30 cases, socialist countries had superior quality of life indicators than capitalist countries of higher economic development. This comprehensive study clearly demonstrates socialist countries have had superior quality of life than capitalist countries. One particular area in which socialism has excelled in providing better quality of life is healthcare. According to the study Has socialism failed? An analysis of health indicators under socialism[2], socialist countries have provided better healthcare outcomes than comparable capitalist countries. To quote the study’s abstract, “contrary to dominant ideology, socialism and socialist forces have been, for the most part, better able to improve health conditions than capitalism and capitalist forces.” When considering quality of life under socialism and capitalism, it’s easy to point to food shortages in the Soviet Union, China, Cuba, and the Eastern Bloc. However, it’s important to consider where these countries started. Russia and Eastern Europe were regularly ravaged by famine prior to becoming socialist. Peasants lived in straw huts and had a life expectancy in the mid 30’s[3]. The fact that socialism took Russia, the feudal backwater of Europe, and became the first country to reach space in three decades is nothing short of incredible. The same applies to Eastern Europe. China is an even more dramatic example of this trend. China, prior to becoming socialist, was incredibly impoverished. Millions died annually from famines, life expectancy was around 30 years old, and literacy was virtually nonexistent. Though Mao and the CCP made their mistakes, they doubled China’s life expectancy[4] in two decades. Cuba is another example of socialism improving quality of life. Before the Cuban Revolution, Cuba was “The Brothel of the Caribbean,” ruled by Miami elites and dominated by American foreign policies. The volunteer literacy brigades, communal farms, and democratic factories created by the communists did wonders for Cuba. The country currently has a higher life expectancy than the United States[5]. Political Freedoms Political freedoms under socialism have been critiqued. However, socialist countries, before becoming socialist, usually had no political freedoms. Before Cuba, China, and the Eastern Bloc became socialist, political freedoms were nonexistent. Cuba was ruled by Fulegncio Bautista, a brutal American puppet who tortured and executed political dissidents. China was a dictatorship, partly ruled by the imperial Japanese army and partly ruled by the brutal Kuomintang. Russia was a Czarist Autocracy, Poland was a fascist dictatorship with concentration camps of their own, and the rest of the Eastern Bloc were brutal autocracies allied with Nazi Germany. Mongolia, Angola, and Vietnam were similar. Socialist countries improved political freedoms in these countries. Cuba is the most democratic country in the Western Hemisphere[6], the Soviet Union held democratic referendums[7], and so on. Although many of these did lack some of the freedoms found in liberal democracies, the freedoms they had were far better than under their previous capitalist rulers. Not to mention, under the Soviet Union, everyone had the freedom to go about life without worrying about eviction, as housing was guaranteed, or about putting food on the table. These freedoms are just as important as freedom of speech or press. Equality Socialist countries have overwhelmingly had less discrimination and inequality than capitalist countries. For example, the Soviet Union made anti-semitism illegal and ended the pogroms perpetrated by the previous Czarist regimes. Many African Americans, fleeing US segregation, even moved to Russia[8], then a bastion of racial equality. That’s not to say that socialist countries. Cuba had discriminatory practices towards LGBTQ+ people in the 1970s, (though it has since apologized[9] and guaranteed full legal rights[10] for LGBTQ+ people), and the Soviet Union had similar horrific practices towards gay people. These policies are utterly inexcusable, however, they were the exception, not the rule. Socialist countries have generally been bastions of equality and respect. Burkina Faso One specific example of an impressive socialist experiment can be found in Burkina Faso from 1983 to 1987. Marxist-Leninist Thomas Sankara came to power on August 4th, 1983. During the course of the next four years, socialist Burkina Faso[11]: -Increased literacy rates 60%, from 13% to 73%, -Planted 10 million trees to successfully stop the southward spread of the Sahara Dessert -Ended River Blindness and Polio, and became the first African country to recognize and take action against AIDS. -Vaccinated millions of children in the first month -Converted an army base into the nation's first supermarket -Greatly reduced government corruption -Sold the government fleet of Mercedes for Renault 5s, the cheapest car available in Burkina Faso at the time -Increased wheat production from 1,700kg/hectare to 3,800kg/hectare -Greatly reduced the amount of bush (rainforest) burning, which was very harmful to the environment -Appointed women to high government positions, encouraged and funded female education, ended polygamy, child marriage, and female genital multination -Decreased reliance on foreign aid -Granted free speech and free press liberties, something absent from the country when he took over -Renamed the country from "Upper Volta" to "Burkina Faso," meaning "Land of the Upright Man" Sadly, Thomas Sankara’s rival Blaise Compaoré, backed by French and American capitalists, launched a coup in 1987 to remove Sankara from power. Though Compaoré succeeded in reversing much of the improvements Sankara’s socialist government achieved, the legacy of Sankara’s stupidly-successful socialist policies remains an inspiration to us all. Capitalist Attacks Of course, these former socialist countries achieved political freedoms and a high quality of life against capitalist attacks and subversion. For example, fourteen countries, including the United States, Japan, England, and Germany invaded the infant Soviet Union in 1919 in an attempt to crush the revolution. Nazi Germany murdered 25 million Russians and destroyed swaths of the country. Cuba has faced similar invasions, economic sanctions, and a blockade. These practices by capitalists have partially succeeded in decimating socialist countries. Laos and Vietnam were never able to become bastions of socialist prosperity because of the US invasion. North Korea was ravaged by American bombers and sanctions. Nicaragua was destabilized by a US-backed terrorist insurgency. Venezuela, which isn’t even socialist, was destroyed by sanctions and coup attempts. Bolivia is currently in the crosshairs of the American empire right now, as it has been targeted by diplomatic vilification and an Elon Musk-backed[12] coup attempt. Yet still, socialist countries have still managed to provide a higher quality of life than capitalist countries. Double standards It’s also interesting how anti-communists view the failures of capitalist countries compared to those of socialist countries. Whenever hardships emerge in a socialist country, it’s always the fault of socialism. However, when capitalist countries suffer famine or brutal dictatorships, it’s never the fault of capitalism. Such hypocrisy is evident over how capitalists view the Nazis. The Nazis were capitalist[13] who practically invented the word “privatization.[14]” However, the 11 million who died in the Holocaust and the many more who died in the Second World War are never tallied as victims of the capitalism. The genocidal tyranny of Suharto or King Leopold or Efraín Ríos Montt are never considered to be the fault of capitalism, for example. The same is true when it comes to famine. 17 million children[15]- or 1 in 4- go to bed hungry every night in America, but that is never the fault of capitalism. If similar statistics were present in a socialist country, it would be on the front page of every anti-communist publication in the world. Similarly, ongoing famine caused by neo-colonialism, over-exploitation of the global south, and the imperialist war in Ukraine is never blamed on capitalism- but if Cuba faced famine similar to that currently present in Ethiopia and Madagascar, it would be immediately blamed on communism. In conclusion, socialism hasn’t failed. Though past socialist experiments have had their flaws, socialist experiments have been successful and superior to capitalism. Solidarity forever, -Ben

Question: Were the Confederate States fascist?
Answer: Well, firstly, we need to define fascism. It’s also to point out that though fascism as a defined ideology began in the early 20th century, that does not mean that fascism didn’t exist. For example, proto-fascist movements in France, such as the anti-dryfusards, existed decades before Mussolini wrote foundational work on fascism. And various Native American tribes, kibbutzs, and Medieval European peasant villages practiced communism long before the creation of Scientific Socialism. Similarly, a state can be fascist without calling themselves fascist. Fascism is, of course, a spectrum, but there are many examples of fascist governments and leaders that do not identify as such. Pinochet’s Chile, Rhodesia, and Giorgia Meloni are such examples. Therefore, it is theoretically possible for the Confederate States of America to be fascist, if they fit the definition. So, how well does the Confederate States of America (CSA) fit the definition of fascism? The Confederacy was extremely militaristic. The army was glorified, and conscription gangs were commonplace in Confederate territories. Obviously the Confederacy was at war for it’s entire existence, so it’s difficult to say how militaristic the CSA would have been in absence of conflict, but during their existence they were very militaristic. The Confederacy was also a dominance of the most reactionary elements of capitalism. The Civil War was fought because wealthy plantation owners wanted to extract the most possible surplus value from their workers through slavery. The plantation owners, who ruled the country, wanted to preserve their class interests through slavery. This slavery was based on an explicit racial hierarchy, similar to the ones practiced by Mussolini, Rhodesia, the Nazis. Lastly, and most importantly, the Confederacy was based on a cult of tradition. The Confederacy claimed it was fighting a war to preserve its traditional (and vile) way of life. The Confederacy glorified a mythic version of America’s founding fathers and their devotion to slavery. Their rabid desire to preserve their traditional way of life is certainly fascist. In conclusion, yes, the Confederate States of America was definitely fascist. Neo-confederates are even more fascist, as they take glorification of a mythic past to a new level are are often associated with Neo-Nazi hate groups. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Was Che Guevara a hero or a tyrant? What do you think about it?
Answer: Che Guevara was a hero. In order to explain why Che Guevara was a hero, I’ll tell the story of his life, then debunk some common attacks against Guevara. Che Guevara was born to a well-off family in Argentina. Studying to be a medical student, Guevara decided to tour South America on his motorbike. Traveling around the continent, Guevara witnessed incredible poverty, destitution, and privation. These conditions convinced Guevara that being a doctor wasn’t for him. After all, you can’t prescribe medicine to cure systemic poverty, racism, or colonialism. Guevara desired to free the world from the clutches of imperialism and capitalism, and he realized communism was the best way to do so. A young Che Guevara Guevara’s communist sympathies were further nurtured in Guatemala. While staying in Guatemala, a US coup overthrew the democratically elected president Jacobo Árbenz. The CIA then instituted a dictatorship that harshly repressed critics while serving the interests of American corporations, specifically the United Fruit Company (now known as the Chiquita banana company). Fleeing the Guatemalan dictatorship, Guevara arrived in Mexico, where he met Fidel and Raul Castro, two exiled Cuban revolutionaries. See, Cuba at the time was a colony of the United States in all but name. Ruled by brutal dictator Fulgencio Batista, the island was a playground for wealthy American tourists. Most of the inhabitants of the island lived in poverty. Amenities like water and electricity were non-existent for most people, and literacy was rare. Guevara and the Castro brothers resolved to liberate Cuba from the clutches of American imperialism. The three comrades, alongside 80 other revolutionaries, landed in the town of Niquero in 1956. Though facing deadly government attacks, including one that cut the revolutionaries’ number down to 20 soldiers, the Cuban rebels persisted in their fight against the government. Soon, with massive popular support, Guevara and the Castro brothers were at the helm of a full-on revolution that threatened the Cuban state and American interests. In 1959, the Cuban rebels finally won the war and toppled the Batista government, making Cuba a socialist state. Guevara was instrumental in turning Cuba from a capitalist economy to a truly workers’s state. Guevara lead volunteer literacy brigades that taught many peasants how to read, and helped defend Cuba against American imperialism during the Bay of Pigs Invasion. However, Guevara was an internationalist, and in 1965 left Cuba for other projects. In the Congo, Guevara lead a team of Cuban advisors to assist communist rebels in taking over the country. Sadly, Guevara failed, and the rebellion was defeated. Unfettered, Guevara left the Congo for Bolivia, where he tried again to lead a communist insurgency. This, however, failed as well, and soon Guevara found himself captured by the Bolivian army and CIA. Not wanting Guevara to escape and lead revolutions elsewhere, the CIA executed Guevara by shooting him in the chest. Moments before dying, Guevara gave his famous last words “Shoot, coward! You are only going to kill a man!" Indeed, Guevara’s words were prophetic. Che Guevara is now a symbol of revolutionary zeal across the world. From Bolivia to Angola to Cuba, murals, statues, and signs proudly show the face of one of the world’s most heroic revolutionaries. Guevara’s contributions to the planet can be felt everywhere. The Cuban Revolution transformed Cuba from a poverty-stricken mess to a developed nation. Currently, Cuba’s literacy right is one of the highest in the world[1], it has the highest doctor/patient ratio in the world[2], and has a longer life expectancy than the United States[3][4]. Cuba even has a higher sustainable development ranking than the United States[5], despite 60 years of brutal American sanctions and an economic blockade designed to cause starvation and unrest[6]. The effects of the Cuban revolution can be felt outside of Cuba, too. In Brazil, Cuban doctors provide medical care to 33,000,000 people[7]. And across Africa, Cuban soldiers helped free many nations from colonial rule. Cuban internationalism, especially in Angola and Namibia, was crucial to dismantling South African apartheid[8]. Cuban soldiers fighting for African liberation If you consider Che’s egalitarianism, selflessness, and intelligence, and consider that Che made the world a much better place, then there’s no way you can argue Che Guevara is not one of the most heroic figures of the 20th century. Debunking anti-Guevara arguments The ruling class, however, knew how powerful of a symbol Guevara was. Wishing to protect their interests, the capitalist class fabricated allegations against Guevara to defame his legacy. I’ll run through some of most common anti-Guevara arguments and debunk them. “Guevara executed innocent civilians” The claim Che Guevara executed innocent civilians is incorrect. Che Guevara did preside over many trials after the Cuban Revolution. However, no civilians were killed. The only people executed were the most brutal torturers of the Batista regime, who murdered civilians and burnt villages[9]. Like those convicted at the Nuremberg Trials, the few people Guevara killed deserved to die. Additionally, those executed were given fair trials. There were lawyers for the prosecution and defense, witnesses were called, and juries were held. The executions were hardly a summary affair or an example of revolutionary justice. “Guevara made Cuba a horrific dictatorship” This claim is also incorrect. Contrary to what CIA-funded NGO’s might tell you, Cuba is actually fairly democratic[10]. The Cuban government permits protests, holds free and accountable elections, and holds forums to receive feedback from the government. In fact, when protests do occur, rather than sending police officers to disrupt the protests, the Cuban government has begun sending elected officials to listen to the people’s demands[11]. “Guevara sent LGBTQ+ people to concentration camps” This claim is incorrect. See, in the late 1960s, Cuba instituted a policy where men could either chose to serve in the military or join work brigades, called UMAPs. UMAPs were offered as a way to defend Cuba without facing active combat in the military.[12] Since LGBTQ+ people weren’t allowed to serve in the military, they were forced to join theUMAPs. This homophobic policy by the Cuban government was wrong and inexcusable. However, the UMAPs had fine conditions and were were far from the concentration camps they’re portrayed as, nor were they targeted at LGBTQ+ people. Additionally, Fidel Castro has since apologized[13] for Cuba’s actions during that time period, and took steps to repair the damage he did. Currently, Cuba now has great civil rights for LGBTQ+ people[14]. Besides, Che Guevara wasn’t even in Cuba when UMAPs were in place. Che Guevara left Cuba well before Castro implemented the UMAP system. So unless you think Che Guevara somehow was calling the shots in Cuba while fighting the CIA with a smelly band of Bolivian rebels, he bears no responsibility for the actions of Cuba’s government at the time. In conclusion, Che Guevara was a heroic figure who liberated Cuba from colonial oppression. He also looks great on a t-shirt. Stay safe, -Ben _ Great Che Guevara tribute song:

Question: What is the easiest and most simple way to explain the differences between left and right wing politics?
Answer: Great question. Firstly, it’s important that we understand the history of the terms left and right. During the French Revolution, when the revolutionary parliament was assembled, different groups of politicians sat in different places. The monarchists who wanted to preserve the old social order sat on the right, and the revolutionaries who wanted a new order sat on the left. Hence, the terms left and right were coined. Those on the political right, generally speaking, wish to preserve the old world order. They are conservative. Just as the people who sat on the right of the revolutionary parliament wanted to preserve the French Monarchy, rightists today want to preserve existing societal institutions, whether that be capitalism, heteronormativity, or the military. Leftists, however, support progressive politics. Leftists want to move society forward, to change things. For example, leftists like myself seek to destroy capitalism, abolish the patriarchy, and defund the police. Capitalism, the patriarchy, and the police are all existing societal institutions protected by many on the right. Of course, politics is rarely this simple. The political spectrum- which you could make a good argument for being outdated- is nuanced and mutifaceted. Many groups support some progressive ideas and not others. Many social democrats, for example, while supporting LGBTQ+ and women’s rights, are opposed to dismantling capitalism. Conservative “communists” like Haz Al-Din seek to uphold the capitalist superstructure while changing its material basis- an idea that’s doomed to fail. Additionally, “left” and “right” are relative. There is no objective leftism or rightism- these terms depend on the context in which they are used. Progressive in the French Revolution would be considered conservative if they were alive today. In 200 years, my leftist politics will hopefully seem conservative. So, that’s the difference between left and right. In practice, leftists often target hierarchies- the hierarchy of employer over employee, of man over women, of white over black- while conservatives defend these hierarchies. Stay safe, -Ben

He nicely summarized his political positions in a letter to his girlfriend, saying: I am much more socialistic in my economic theory than capitalistic… capitalism has outlived its usefulness.[1] See, King understood that the oppression faced by black people was inherently linked the oppression of capitalism. Capitalism and racism have a co-dependent relationship, and abolishing the one must mean abolishing the other. And the greed and exploitation which creates the sector of poverty in the midst of wealth. Again, we have deluded ourselves into believing the myth that capitalism grew and prospered out of the protestant effort of hard work and sacrifice. The fact is that capitalism was built on the exploitation and suffering of black slaves, and continues to thrive on the exploitation of the poor, both black and white, both here and abroad. And we must also realize that the problems of racial injustice and economic injustice cannot be solved without a radical redistribution of political and economic power. We must further recognize that the ghetto is a domestic colony. Black people must create programs that will aid in the transfer of power and wealth into the hands of the residents of the ghetto so that they may in reality control their own destinies.[2] -MLK Malala Yousafzai Malala Yousafzai is a Pakistani activist for the rights of women and girls. However, this attempted murder only amplified Malala, who’s since won a Nobel Peace Prize. However, few know that Malala is also a socialist. In a letter to a group of Pakistani Marxists, she wrote: I am convinced Socialism is the only answer and I urge all comrades to take this struggle to a victorious conclusion. Park’s refusal to move to the back of a segregated bus sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, which played an important role in bringing segregation to its knees. However, Rosa Parks also held socialist views. She attended meetings of the Communist Party, which at the time was one of the strongest forces fighting for racial equality[4]. Albert Einstein Albert Einstein is undoubtedly one of the smartest people to have ever existed. The word “Einstein” is synonymous with genius. But in addition to being a brilliant physicist and mathematician, Einstein was also a hardcore socialist. Einstein even published an essay, “Why Socialism?[5]” in which he advocated for a post-capitalist world. He also praised Lenin, stating I honor Lenin as a man who completely sacrificed himself and devoted all his energy to the realization of social justice. I do not consider his methods practical, but one thing is certain: men of his type are the guardians and restorers of the conscience of humanity. Frida Khalo and Diego Rivera Frida Khalo was already mentioned in the question, but she and her estranged husband Diego Rivera were communists. The ideals of the Mexican Revolution greatly shaped Khalo especially, and she was a card-carrying member of the Mexican Communist Party for most of her life. Khalo even had an affair with Leon Trotsky while he was exiled in Mexico[6]. Nelson Mandela I know Nelson Mandela was also mentioned in the question, but I’d like to touch on Mandela’s political beliefs. Nelson Mandela was a hardcore Communist. Unlike the peace-loving reconciliatory figure we often imagine him as, Mandela was a militant activist willing to die for socialism. In fact, in response to the Sharpsville Massacre, in which South African government troops fired upon masses of peaceful protestors, Mandela created an armed insurgency. Question: What do Marxists mean when they use the phrase "contradictions in capitalism"? What are some examples of these contradictions, and why should we worry about them? Do you wish the primitive accumulation had not happened?
Answer: Firstly, we’ll need to examine what a contradiction is. In Marxist terms, a contradiction is when there are two opposing forces acting against each other. Marxists like to analyze contradictions using dialectical materialism- that is, looking at the contradictions within a concept while recognizing said contradictions are in constant motion. Marxists have found many contradictions within capitalism. Although there are hundreds of contradictions in capitalism, I’ll look at some of the three most stark contradictions. Firstly, there is the contradiction between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. The bourgeoisie tries to get rich by taking the surplus value of the proletariat. The proletariat does not want their surplus value to be taken, and so develops class antagonisms between the ruling class and the working class. This class conflict is the largest contradiction within capitalism. Another contradiction in capitalism is in worker wages. Profit is gained through the extraction of surplus value, and capitalists are motivated to extract more surplus value to increase profits. However, decreasing wages too much, in addition to causing class antagonisms, leads to less disposable income for workers. Workers then can’t purchase as many products, which means capitalists receive less money. We’re currently seeing this contradiction between the desire to extract surplus value and the need for disposable income play out right now in the United States. Lastly, I’ll cover the contradictions that come with unemployment. Capitalists wish to extract the most surplus value possible, and to do so employing as many people as possible is optimal. However, capitalists also need a reserve army of labor to bully workers into accepting subpar working conditions. (If there’s a group of homeless, unemployed people with nothing to lose willing to accept worse working conditions, you’ll be a lot less likely to protest an increase in hours and a decrease in wages). These opposing forces- the desire to extract maximum surplus value vs the need for a reserve army of labor) constitute a contradiction. So, those are three of the contradictions of capitalism. These contradictions exude poverty, homelessness, and starvation for the working class while lining the pockets of the ruling class, and we must overthrow capitalism to reconcile these contradictions. With regards to the primitive accumulation of capital, I don’t believe I’m well educated enough on that subject to say whether I wish it had happened or not. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Can socialism actually work within a capitalist economy?
Answer: No. Socialism is defined as worker control over the means of production, the abolition class, and the distribution of goods to meet human needs rather than profit. Capitalism is defined as private ownership of the means of production, and is characterized by a strict, hierarchical class division between the working class and the ruling class. The profit motive is all consuming. As you can see, these economic situations are not compatible. You cannot have a dictatorship of the proletariat, in which the sole class and ruling class is the working class, and the class divisions of capitalism. You cannot both manufacture goods to meet human needs and profit, because profit incentives rarely align with human needs. And you cannot have the average workers control the means of production while having a tiny minority of people control the means of production at once. Capitalism and socialism are not mutually compatible. One common misconception about socialism is that “socialism is when the government does stuff.” That is incorrect, as government intervention in the economy can occur in capitalist countries. Social democracies, such as those found in the Nordic Countries, are capitalist with a strong social safety net. In conclusion, socialism cannot work in a capitalist economy. In order to achieve a better world, we must immediately dismantle capitalism and achieve worker control of the means of production. We must kill capitalism before it kills us. Stay safe, -Ben

Oligarch Elon Musk, known for his illegal union-busting tactics, usage of child labor in Central Africa, and general douchiness Socialism, however, has a democratic workplace organization. Either through a democratically elected state or through co-operative enterprises, under socialism, workers own the means of production. This system is far more fair and democratic than capitalism. Plus, without the constant need for profit to sate shareholder demands, these enterprises are also more resilient to changes in external economic conditions[1]. Profit In the employer/employee relationship inherent to capitalism, some value generated by the employee is taken by the employer in the form of profit. This profit is known as the worker’s “surplus value.” Essentially, the worker generates some value that is then taken by the employer, who does not compensate the employee for said value. This practice is exploitative. The worker is being paid less than the value of their labor is worth. The view that wage labor was little better than chattel slavery was common in the 19th century, espoused by people such as Fredrick Douglas and organizations such as the Lowell Mill Girls However, under socialism, there is no employer to take surplus value. Workers could get to vote how much of the value they generate for their enterprise is invested into expanding and growing the enterprise and how much is returned to the worker. This system is far fairer and more democratic, rather than the authoritarianism of capitalism. Capitalism’s drive for profit is also morally wrong. I’ve gone into it in more depth in another answer[2], but capitalism is the reason we have both millions of people dying of hunger and enough food to easily feed those people. Under socialism, actions that aren’t necessarily profitable but are still morally right would be committed, like giving vaccines to impoverished countries that can’t afford to purchase them. The Environment Capitalism is based off of infinite growth in a finite world. Is it any surprise, then, that under capitalism we are living in a man-made environmental extinction event? Socialism, meanwhile, respects the limits of the natural world. It doesn’t have the need to constantly open new markets, the environment be damned. Additionally, democratic workplaces are far better for the environment than capitalist enterprises. Under capitalism, the employer makes all the decisions regarding his company- including it’s environmental impact. The employer is usually quite wealthy, and therefore has the means to survive environmental catastrophe, unlike his employees. As a result, the employer will likely take steps to increase their profit at the expense of the environment, given that said employer will likely not suffer from environmental destruction. Who will suffer from environmental devestation? The everyday workers. If the workers control the means of production and get to decide how an enterprise is run, they’ll respect the environment a lot more, since they have a dog in the hunt. Therefore, socialism is better for the environment than capitalism. Historical Evidence Opponents of socialism love to point out so called “failures” of socialism. We can go back in forth about whether this or that country was really socialist, but several key facts remain. Firstly, capitalism failed every time it was tried for the first 300 years of its existence (before promptly geocoding the entire North American continent). Socialism has existed for only 150 years, give or take a couple decades. Socialists have been continuing learning from our mistakes and improving our socialist experiments. Secondly, socialist countries in the past have provided superior quality of life and healthcare than capitalist countries. This claim is backed by numerous peer-reviewed studies[3][4]. Thirdly, there have been socialist/communist countries that have become dictatorships. To pretend otherwise is to be blinded by one’s own ideals. However, just as we shouldn’t pretend that North Korea or Cuba are democratic paradises, we shouldn’t ignore the external factors that influenced their development[5]. Particularly Cuba has been under attack militarily, economically, and diplomatically from the strongest country ever to exist on earth. Despite this enormous obstacle, it still has a superior healthcare system to the United States and a longer life expectancy. In early 2020, Italy pled for doctors to help them deal with the COVID-19 pandemic, and Cuba responded by shipping dozens of excellently trained doctors to Italy to help fight the pandemic Debunking counterarguments: “No iPhone” The technology behind the iPhone was developed in the public sector. In fact, according to economist Mariana Mazzucato, every major technological innovation in recent years traces its funding back to the state. This fact makes sense. Private companies are notoriously bad at developing entirely new technologies. Technological research is slow and oftentimes unproductive, and companies find it difficult to justify to their shareholders why they’re investing in a research project that may or may not come to fruition in 30 years or so. It’s usually not very profitable to research new technologies. It’s only when the government provides funding that new breakthroughs happen. Introducing: the ourPhone “X socialist country became a dictatorship” Yes, there are socialist countries that committed horrible atrocities. But it would be disingenuous to state that these dictators represent all of socialism. There are examples of successful socialist experiments. For example, while Burkina Faso was socialist from 1983 to 1987, it raised the literacy rate 60%, made massive strides towards gender equality, and put a stop to government corruption. More recently, Rojava, a collection of autonomous communities in Northeastern Syria defeated ISIS, achieved full gender equality, and gave representation to historically oppressed ethnic minorities. All of these achievements came while avoiding a major food crisis, despite an influx of 1.5 million refugees from the Syrian Civil War. Besides, I could always point out evil capitalist countries. Adolf Hitler was a capitalist. So was Suharto. Pol Pot was backed by the CIA. Despotic dictators are not unique to socialism- in fact, they’re more common under capitalism. Authoritarian control of the workplace lends itself more easily to authoritarian control of government. Even countries anti-socialists like to cite as failures of socialism, like Mao’s China and the USSR, while certainly flawed, had many impressive achievements. The USSR went from using wooden plows to conquering the cosmos in 3 decades, and Mao’s China had a lower death rate than similar developing nations[6]. “Less incentive to work” Firstly, under socialism, people would work less. That’s a good thing. Under socialism, technological innovations make human’s lives easier, whereas under capitalism, technological innovations serve only profit. To quote Peter Kropotkin, in his superb essay An Appeal to the Young, Under the domination of private property and wage-slavery, every new invention only makes his slavery heavier, his labor more degrading, the periods of slack work more frequent, the crisis sharper, and that the man who already has every conceivable pleasure for himself is the only one who profits by it. Remember, with no surplus value being kept by someone who “already has every conceivable pleasure for himself,” workers receive more value from their work. This increases the incentive to work (one gets more output) while reducing the amount of work necessary to have a fulfilling life. In conclusion, socialism is the clearly superior economic system. Question: What are the most important battles of the recent past (since 2000)?
Answer: One important battle was the Siege of Kobani. In 2011, the Arab Spring sent Syria into a death spiral. Dozens of armed groups, from the FSA (Free Syrian Army) and the al-Nursa front (Al Qaeda) began to attack the Syrian government, leading to a brutal conflict that left thousands dead in its first year. One of the few bright spots to emerge from Syria, however, was the Rojava Revolution. Inspired by the ideas of feminism, libretarian socialism, ecology, and democratic confederalism espoused by the imprisoned revolutionary Abdullah Occalan, the mainly Kurdish revolution spread across Northern Syria, providing a safe haven for refugees fleeing conflict elsewhere in the country. The YPG, people’s protection units who made up the military of Rojava, fought pitched battles against FSA forces and forged a tentative alliance with the Syrian Government. But Rojava was soon eclipsed by another rising force- the Islamic State. After successfully taking the Anbar region of Iraq, ISIS, or Daesh as the Kurds call it, spread into Syria and soon became the dominant force in the region. Rojava and ISIS were natural enemies. ISIS’s intsenly sexist ideals clashed with the YPG’s feminism; a parrallel military structure, called the YPJ and composed solely of female fighters made up a signifigant portion of Rojava’s military. Additionally, though inspired by Muslim cultures, Rojava was largely secular, as opposed to ISIS’s religious jihadism. Throughout the summer of 2014, Rojava found its territory quickly collapsed under an intense ISIS assault. By September, Rojava had been split in two- the Kobani canton had been completely isolated from the de facto Rojava capital of Qamislo, and the territory surrounding it. If Kobani, a culturally significant Kurdish city, fell, the war would essentially be over for Rojava, and ISIS would rule supreme in Northern Syria. Recognizing this fact, ISIS launched a massive assault on Kobani, employing over 9,000 fighters against several thousand outgunned Kurds. The YPG fought hard, but with Turkey, Kobani’s neighbor to the north, refusing to allow Kurdish volunteers to travel to Rojava to fight, the situation seemed hopeless. ISIS occupied more than 50% of Kobani by mid-October. A Kurdish fighter in Kobani But mid-October would mark the high water mark of the Islamic State. Coalition airstrikes decimated ISIS armored forces during a series of intense bombing runs between October 13th and 15th. Caving to international pressure, Turkey begrudgingly allowed Kurdish fighters to travel to Kobani to fight, including several hundred heavily armed Peshmerga forces. This arrival marked a near-complete end to the tension present in relations between Peshmerga and Rojava. Most importantly, however, a YPG/YPJ counterattack retook major portions of the town. Coalition airstrikes As 2014 ended and 2015 began, the YPG slowly retook portions of the now ruined city. By January, Islamic State positions had completely collapsed, by February the entire city had been liberated. The importance of Kobani cannot be overstated. The Islamic State, having previously seemed invincible, had now suffered a major defeat. The Rojava Revolution had been reinvigorated, and the tactical initiative had been regained. YPG fighters celebrate their victory 2015 saw the YPG and YPJ merge with smaller groups into the Syrian Democratic Forces, a coalition of socialist, feminist, and anarchist forces allied against ISIS. Rojava severed the road between ISIS’s largest strongholds, Mosul and Raqqa, during the Awl Hawl offensive in 2015, and 2016 saw Manjib fall. In 2017, Mosul fell to Iraqi and Peshmerga forces, and Rojava liberated Raqqa in 2017. By 2019 ISIS had lost all of its territorial holdings in Syria, though an insurgency continues to this day in liberated territories. International volunteers also played a major war in the war against the Islamic State, such as these anarcho-communists That said, Kobani remained the graveyard of many YPG fighters and civilians alike. Despite being crucial to turning the tide of the war against the Islamic State, the battle was still a tragedy, as thousands of innocent Kurdish civilians lost their lives and hundreds of thousands were displaced, and 70% of the city was destroyed. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What is the biggest problem with capitalism?
Answer: There are many problems with capitalism, but to me the biggest is the drive for profit. In order to understand how harmful the drive for profit can be, we need to understand two basic facts. The first is that profit is the primary motivator under capitalism. The second is that competition in the “free market” is intense and merciless- people’s livelihoods are at stake, after all. Firstly, under capitalism, it’s actively discouraged to do anything that isn’t profitable. Since competition is so ruthless and cutthroat, capitalists spend every ounce of energy focused on maximizing profit. Any action that hurts profits is therefore discouraged, as it lowers one’s competitive advantage. However, many rational and moral actions are not profitable, and therefore discouraged. One example is providing food to people who cannot afford it. We have a surplus of food in the United States, enough to feed everyone in the nation easily. In fact, many farmers have so much food they are destroying it[1]. However, as many as 14 million children in the United States do not get enough to eat on a daily basis[2] because they cannot afford food. It is not profitable to give food to these children who cannot afford it, despite obviously being the moral thing to do. Therefore, providing food to starving children is discouraged under capitalism, as that action harms profit. This example is only one of many. Giving vaccines to the global south, housing the homeless, and preparing for global pandemics[3] are all rational and moral actions, but are not undertaken (except by a few charities) because they are not profitable. This drive for profit also causes capitalists to commit evil actions. The United Fruit Company, for example, committed horrendous actions in Latin America[4] because it was profitable to do so. Corporations in the Democratic Republic of Congo use 4-year old child laborers[5] in unsafe cobalt mines because it is profitable to do so. Elon Musk attempted a coup of Bolivia[6] to get better deals on lithium because it was profitable to do so. The list goes on and on. Mining for cobalt in the DRC These actions are encouraged under capitalism. As nice as it is to say that cheaters never win in the end, that assertion is simply false. People who cut corners, use shady methods, and bend moral principles make more profit under capitalism than those who do not. In the cutthroat competition inherent to capitalism, people more willing to tale nefarious actions to succeed will win out over those who stand by moral principles. The aforementioned shady capitalists will then continue to use corrupt methods to gain more profit, reproducing the problem of unscrupulous capitalists. In conclusion, the drive for profit is my biggest issue with capitalism. There are many more problems with the system- the falling rate of profit and the contradiction between use value and exchange value chief among them- but the drive for profit is my greatest problem with the system. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What is antifa?
Answer: Antifa is simply the idea of being against fascism. In this history, I’ll briefly explore the history, organization (or lack thereof) and ideology of antifascism, shorted to “antifa” by some, as well as debunk some myths about them. History Antifas developed along proto-fascism in France in the late 1890s, during the Dryfus Affair. Proto-fascists, known as antidryfusards, tried to convict the Jewish officer Alfred Dryfus on trumped-up accounts of treason, while Dryfusards tried to defend him. While the Dryfusards did successfully exonerate Dryfus, the first seeds of fascism were born, in the right-wing organization Action Française. As fascism grew during the early 20th century, there were always anti-fascists to fight back. But some of these movements were stronger than others. For example, in Italy, the anti-fascist movement was pathetically weak, with some groups plainly capitulating to Mussolini before the fascists had even taken power. This failure left the majority of the work to stop fascism to the liberal Italian government, which was promptly taken over by Mussolini. To anti-fascists, this simply illustrated the failure of parlimentary methods to stop fascism. Anti-fascists began fighting fascists in the streets. One notable instance was on April 15th, 1925, when communist anti-fascists ambushed a large group of French fascists after dark. When the dust finally settled, four fascists were dead and thirty more wounded. More fighting would follow. In Germany, two anti-fascist organizations, Antifaschistische Aktion and the Iron Front, took up arms to stop the Nazis in the early 1930s. These two organizations fought Nazis (and sometimes each other) in violent gun battles across Germany. When the Nazis came to power, it turned out the Iron Front was made of tin, and so collapsed. Antifaschistische Aktion went underground. Following the Allied victory in the Second World War, fascism became less overt, though still everpresent. The 43 Group, a collection of British Jewish World War Two veterans, fought fascists lead by Oswald Mosely in the streets of London, eventually defeating Mosely’s fascists. Rock and Roll in the 1970s became a battleground between antifascist and fascist skinheads. Since the 70s, the battles have mostly moved to Europe, notably in Scandinavia, where antifascists stopped the rise of several fascist groups. Notably, antifascists won a major victory when the Greek Neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn was labeled a criminal organization. Today, antifascists continue to combat fascists across the world. They Shall Not Pass, and the Battle of Cable Street One of the most notable antifascist slogans is “They shall not pass.” The phrase was first used by Marshal Philippe Pétain during the French defense of Verdun. Since then, it’s been used as a symbol of resistance by antifascist forces. Notably, it was used by communist forces at the Battle of Madrid during the Spanish Civil War after the successful defense of the city. However, it’s most famous usage came during the Battle of Cable Street. They did not pass! Fascism wants to conquer Madrid. Madrid will be the tomb of fascism In 1936, Oswald Mosely, leader of the fascist Blackshirts in England, organized a march through the Jewish section of the East End in London, with police protection, to terrorize the Jewish population. Opposing them was a union of antifascists, communists, Jews, trade unionists, and even the Mafia. Heavy fighting ensued, with several thousand fascists and police trying to break the antifascist lines of barricades. However, the antifascists held the line, using the phrase “They shall not pass.” Methods Antifascists believe that liberal democracies are not able to stop fascism. Instead, antifascists believe that violence is an acceptable response to fascism. That said, 97% of antifascist actions are nonviolent, such as making community gardens, putting up posters, and playing music over fascist marches. Antifascists believe that violence is opposed on us every day by the capitalist system, and that violence is at times necessary response to fascism. Richard Spencer, a neo-Nazi leader, getting what he deserves Organization There is no formal Antifa organization. Antifa is an idea, an ideology, a philosophy, not an organization. Like how there are various fascist groups in various countries, there are various Antifascist groups in various countries. To say that something that applies to one antifascist group applies to all antifascists is wrong, as antifascism is a diverse tradition spanning many generations and countries. Free Speech Many critics have attacked antifascists for denying Nazis and fascists the right to free speech. Given that the First Amendment in the United States protects free speech solely from government infringement, it is understood on the ground that free speech is an inherent basic right, like the right to exist. However, fascists attempt to stifle other’s free speech. Fascist governments, whether they be Pinochet’s Chile, Franco’s Spain, or Hitler’s Germany, trample on the free speech of innocent civilians, who did not chose to join an evil ideology. For that reason, antifascists feel justified in deplatforming fascists. The three arrows is an antifascist symbol first used by the SPD in the early 1930s. It was developed because it could be drawn over Nazi swaztikas, altering the meaning of the symbol to one of anti-fascism Just as bad as Nazis… Antifascists have been compared to fascists and Nazis in that antifascists seek to deplatform fascists. It has also been suggested that antifascists might convert people to Nazis by gaining sympathy for the Nazis when a Nazi is punched by an antifascist. However, the worst parts of fascism and Naziism isn’t deplatforming terrorists. Fascist regimes do far, far worse things like genocide. To compare punching a Nazi to committing genocide is intellectually dishonest and disrespectful to those who suffered under the Nazis. Additionally, if seeing a Nazi being punched makes someone a Nazi, then antifascists don’t want that person on their side. That person obviously isn’t thinking clearly. So, I hope you’ve leared something about Antifa. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Which battle of the American Revolution was most pivotal in the eventual outcome?
Answer: There are several excellent answers here, that cover important battles such as Kings Mountain and Saratoga. While this battle was not quite as pivotal as these, it was an essential point in the war that is almost never talked about. This battle was the Battle of Assunpink Creek, also known as the Second Battle of Trenton, which took place in between the First Battle of Trenton and Princeton. Essentially, it saw a force lead by George Washington fight off repeated British assaults that threatened to destroy the Continental Army. Following the crucial American victory at the Battle of Trenton, the Continental Army was in no means in the clear. The Americans, though morale was high, were underfed and undermanned. Additionally, British general William Howe was bearing down on Washington’s Army with a massive force. By January 2nd, 1777, Washington found himself in an unenviable position. His 7,000 men at Trenton would meet the full force of General Howe’s army shortly- however, they couldn’t retreat, as they wouldn’t have time to cross the ice-clogged Deleware River to escape to Pennsylvania before Howe reached them. Washington understood that if Howe won a decisive victory here at Trenton, he could erase Washington’s previous victory the week prior. He would then march on Philadelphia that winter, forcing the Continental Congress to sue for peace. American General Jospeh Reed, however, had other ideas. Having grown up around Trenton, he realized that the Continental Forces could make a stand at the Assunpink Creek behind Trenton, the only crossing of the creek being a narrow stone bridge. Washington could make a stand there. And that’s what Washington did. He positioned his army behind the bridge, and the British launched repeated attacks to try to cross the bridge. However, Washingon stood firm, bravely leading his men from the front and holding the line. One soldier, John Howland of Rhode Island, noted The firm, composed, and majestic countenance of the general inspired confidence and assurance in a moment so important and critical. I was pressed against the shoulder of the general’s horse and in contact with the general’s boot. The horse stood firm as the rider, and seemed to understand that he was not to quit his post and station. Indeed, Washington’s leadership helped the Continental Army win the day. Grapeshot tore through repeated British efforts to cross the bridge. Within an hour, 365 British soldiers lay dead, while the Americans suffered only 55 casualties. The importance of Assunpink Creek cannot be overstated. Had Washington’s forces not held the line, the war could have been lost. Nathaniel Philbrick’s book, Valiant Ambition, says the following: If the British manahged to force their way across the bridge and overrun the American army, the war was as good as finished… at the Second Battle of Trenton Washington’s natural agressiveness had succeeded in turning a potential catastrophe of his own devising into an improbable triumph. Indeed, thanks to the Battle of Assunpink the Continent Army had been bought a night of respit before the British attacked the next day. Washington used this break to sneak around the British lines, escaping his perilous predicament and winning a stunning victory at Princeton the next day. After that, the revitalized Continental Army would spend a relaxed winter at Morristown, and continue the fight against the British. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: How did Gilead Paelleon die?
Answer: He was assassinated during the Battle of Fondor. See, the Galactic Alliance, lead by Jacen Solo and Cha Niathal (the two were Joint Chiefs of State) were at war with the Confederation in the year 41 ABY. Though the Alliance had seen success, and the tide was currently, in their favor, the Alliance’s advance was slow and their forces spread thin across the galaxy. Solo decided that a way to achieve a breakthrough victory would be to take out the planet Fondor. Fondor was the Confederation’s largest shipyard, and had been producing ships for the war effort nonstop since the fighting had begun a year ago. However, in order to get enough ships for the large push on Fondor, the Alliance needed the support of the Imperial Remnant, lead by Gilead Paelleon and the Moff Council. Pressured by the Moff Council, Paelleon agreed that the Imperial Remnant would help take Fondor- in exchange for Borelias and Bilbringi, two planets known for their banking and shipbuilding, respectively. However, wary of Solo, Paelleon called for an old friend who owed him an important debt- Natasi Daala, who had gone missing and was presumed dead 23 years earlier during the Battle of Champala. The Galactic Alliance and Imperial Remnant forces attacked Fondor and , despite initial setbacks, saw great success, smashing through the Confederation defenses and establishing aerial dominance over the planet. In order to force Fondor to surrender, Solo, (now a Sith Lord) began firing on the civilian centers of Fondor. Even after the Fondorians surrendered, Solo continued his bombardment, killing millions. Disgusted, Niathal turned on Jacen and ordered all Galactic Alliance forces to attack him. However, two thirds of the GA forces sided with Solo. Jacen’s Sith apprentice, Tahiri Veila, was sent to Paelleon’s flagship, the Bloodfin, to demand that Paelleon assist Jacen. Paelleon refused, and Veila threatened him with death if he failed to comply. When Paelleon did not listen to Veila and ordered the Remnant to join Niathal, Veila executed Paelleon. Paelleon’s choice to side with Niathal, even though he knew it would cost him his life, is the conclusion of Paelleon’s multi-book story arc. In 8 ABY, Paelleon had joined Thrawn during his campaign, and later joined a reborn Darth Sidious during Operation Shadow Hand. Paelleon wished to bring about the Empire he viewed had gone up in flames with the Second Darth Star- one that emphasized loyalty and order, yet was just and fair. Paelleon watched the Crimson Empire rise and fall, joining Treutan Teradoc, the largest of the Warlords in the Deep Core. However, Teradoc and the other warlords were worse than the Imperials he had left behind, wasting their soldiers in fruitless battles among the densest-packed stars in the galaxy. Paelleon found hope in Natasi Daala, who lured the Deep Core warlords to Tsoss Beacon before executing the lot of them. However, as Daala wasted her opportunity on a failed attack on the Jedi Praxeum at Yavin IV, Paelleon realized the Empire he had remembered had never existed. Taking command of the remnants of the Crimson Empire and whatever Daala had left behind, Paelleon formed the Imperial Remnant, making peace with the New Republic and making the Empire what he always dreamed of- an orderly, secure, and peaceful state- though an admittedly undemocratic one. At Fondor, however, we see Paelleon truly cement his status as a hero. Paelleon was torn between siding with Jacen Solo- who’s Palpatinian actions symbolized the Empire- and the Mon Calamari Cha Niathal, who represented the New Republic. As Paelleon lay dying and ordered his forces to join Niathal, Palleon finally embraced democracy and the light. Cha Niathal Paelleon’s sacrifice was not in vain. Though the Moffs’ disobeyed Paelleon and joined Solo, Daala, continuing Paelleon’s legacy, arrived with a large armada. Her forces were able to temporarily drive of Solo. Niathal and the Fondorian government formed the Alliance-in-exile, with help from the Jedi Coalition, leaving Jacen Solo- a Sith Lord- in complete control of the Galactic Alliance. Sp, that is the story behind Paelleon’s death at the Battle of Fondor. Stay safe, -Ben

This made Fallujah the bloodiest battle in US military history since Veitnam. Stories of their bravery deserved to be recorded and read by the next generation. Unsung, the noblest deed will die.” The similarities between Felucia and Fallujah are even more interesting when you consider that Fallujah took place during late 2004, only around six months before Revenge of the Sith and Battlefront II came out. The similarities are too apparent for me to write this off as a coincidence. So, to conclude, the Battle of Felucia was almost certainly based off of the real life Battle of Fallujah.
