Name: Ben Choucroun
Question: What did the Rebel Alliance do with captured Imperial soldiers?
Answer: Well, what they did is actually really interesting and ingenious. See, the Alliance had a number of safe worlds across the galaxy. These were planets, typically sparsely populated, that the Empire didn’t know about. The Alliance controlled these worlds, and their populations were citizens of the Rebel Alliance. So, when the Rebels captured Imperial soldiers, they would take them to these safe worlds and put them on an uninhabited continent. The Alliance would then give them enough supplies to survive for a year, along with farm equipment, and then they would leave and never return, save to drop off other prisoners or to send in heavily armed medical craft. This solution is actually brilliant. For one, the Imperial prisoners have no way to build any sort of ships or transportation vehicles to get across or to leave their continent. For another, most safe worlds had little to no spaceships, save for visits from Alliance Support Services to pick up and drop off supplies. (Safe worlds generally produced most of the Alliance’s foodstuffs). So, that is what the Rebel Alliance did with captured Imperial soldiers. Basically, plop them on a continent somewhere with nothing to do but farm and think about their actions. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What happened to Grievous's body after his death?
Answer: In Legends, it became the armor for a combat droid. Following General Grievous’ defeat on Utapau, his body was taken to one of Palpatine’s secret labratories on the planet. There, Grievous’ body became that of an assassin droid, called N-K Necrosis. The droid was quite skilled in lightsaber combat. He wielded Darth Zannahs red double bladed lightsaber, which had once been possessed by Grievous. However, he was eventually defeated by a group of explorers in the Myyydril Caverns, a system of caves under Kashyyyk. I’d imagine that Grievous would not be happy to learn what had happened to his body. Grievous always insisted he was not a droid, and hated the droids he commanded. He would likely consider what happened to his body extremely disrespectful. So, that is what happened to Grievous’ body after his death. Eventually, his would mask would end up in the possession of Grand Admiral Thrawn, who would study it like he did art. Stay safe, -Ben

Name: Ben Choucroun
Question: In Star Wars, how do the blasters work? Do they have magazines or do they have infinite ammo?
Answer: Blasters used pressurized tibanna gas and a power pack. The power pack would pressurize a small amount of tibanna gas, which would then be focused into a bolt. This bolt would be shot out of the weapon at an enemy. Blasters needed two types of ammunition: tibanna gas and a power pack. The power pack only had enough power for a limited number of shots. When the power pack was emptied, like a normal cartridge, it had to be replaced. You can see in the bottom right corner that this power pack has 258 shots left in it The same applies to tibanna gas. However, generally the tibanna gas canister in the gun didn’t have to be refuled very often. This is because tibanna gas very powerful, and only a tiny amount was needed for a blaster shot. Cloud City mined Tibanna gas The amount of gas in a weapon depended on its size. A E-11 blaster, the type commonly wielded by stormtroopers, had 300 shots worth of tibanna gas. Hapan royalty carried a small hold out blaster with two shots- one for an enemy and another because sometimes it was better to dead than captured. So, that is how blasters and their ammo work. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Forget about superweapons, which planet, place or territory in the entire Star Wars Galaxy is the hardest to invade and conquer in a good old slug out fight?
Answer: Coruscant. Now, the reason Coruscant is so hard to capture is because of how big it is. This is because Coruscant has 5,000 levels. That’s 5,000 levels of buildings across the planet that one needs to clear out, 5,000 levels for terrorists or resistance groups to hide. What’s more, space supremacy over Coruscant is difficult to take. For one, Coruscant is usually very heavily guarded, with a planetary shield and orbital defenses. What’s more, the Coruscant system has 10 planets, each of them a place for an enemy fleet to hide behind. These difficulties were so pronounced that no galactic government could truly conquer the Coruscant underworld. Even the Yuuzhan Vong, who terraformed Coruscant and moved its orbit close to its star, could not conquer the Coruscant underworld. So, in conclusion, Coruscant is the hardest planet to capture in Star Wars. Stay safe, -Ben

Name: Ben Choucroun
Question: What is Ben Choucroun opinion on new Canon?
Answer: I don’t hate it. But I don’t love it either. See, there are many aspects of canon that I like. I like Clone Wars, Rebels, the Original Trilogy, and the Prequels. But canon pales in comparison to Legends in almost every aspect. Let’s look at the books. When it comes to canon, almost every single book is a sidestory. There is nothing actually important to the main storyline outside of the movies. The exception is Aftermath, which is so poorly written it had to be intentional. Now, a single side story is by no means bad. But when all of your books are side stories then you have a massive issue. Compare that to Legends. In Legends, we have the Galactic Civil War, Yuuzhan Vong War, Second Galactic Civil War all told in books. We have meaningful stories that impact the universe. And we have characters like Jacen Solo that have a great arc that is told through 20 years of stories, both from an in and out of universe perspective. What’s more, most of Legends is more cohesive and less confusing than canon. In canon, and especially the sequels, you get stuff like Operation Cinder and Palpatine’s return, the Holdo Maneuver and Luke’s character assassination, and the fall of the New Republic. None of this stuff makes any sense, and these are major plot points. In addition, Legends has tiers of canon. So when there is a discrepancy- say, as in what happened right before the Battle of Coruscant- we get an answer. We don’t have that in canon, with contradictions like whether Ahsoka was on Mandalore or not during Order 66. So, in conclusion, I don’t hate canon. But it certainly isn’t as good as Legends. Stay safe, -Ben
